Plasma cleaning serves as an *in situ* method for superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) cavities located inside cryomodules, aimed at reducing field emission levels. Developed originally for the Linac Coherent Light Source II (LCLS-II) cavities, this study details the comprehensive implementation and application of plasma processing to the High Energy (HE) verification cryomodule's (vCM) at LCLS-II. We confirmed the efficacy of our plasma treatment on four of the eight cavities within this cryomodule; the processed cavities retained original performance regarding accelerating field strength and quality factor. Notably, since the vCM consisted of a clean Cryomodule with record-breaking attributes prior to processing, no additional contaminants were detected in the structure, leaving it field emission–free even at each cavity's maximum operational field. Research further reveals a significant reduction—and complete elimination—of multipacting (MP) quenches typically observed in elevated MP bands. Placing such localized plasma processing capabilities into *in situ* workflows suggests substantial advantages: it offers a dual strategy to mitigate both multipacting and field emission, drastically cutting down testing duration, commissioning overheads, expenses, and enhancing overall facility reliability and lifespan significantly.

In developing nations, electricity theft—illegal interference by consumers with their meters to evade charges—is prevalent and detrimental to both utility infrastructures and society at large. Consequently, various automated systems employing user consumption data have been introduced to detect malpractice; yet, these approaches often prove inadequate due to the wide variety in theft strategies and the inconsistent patterns of user behavior. To address these limitations, this study proposes a multi-source data methodology for identifying theft. Beyond traditional meter readings, this approach incorporates regional metrics (non-technical loss) and climatic variables (temperature specific to a transformer's geographic area). Analytic experiments revealed distinct behaviors; specifically, thieves tend to exhibit significantly higher energy consumption than averages during periods of extreme thermal conditions. Guided by this insight, a new hierarchical framework was developed to classify offenders. Validation on real-world data indicates that this model outperforms standard benchmarks in theft detection, yielding improvements of at least 3.0% in terms of F0.5 scores. Ultimately, this system is operational within China's State Grid and has been successfully deployed in Hangzhou to identify thieves during monthly field audits. During this pilot, a precision enhancement from near-zero adoption (prior models) to 15% was observed using the proposed methodology.

The loss function stands as one of the most crucial hyperparameters in a neural network, and with the myriad of designs available, selecting the correct one remains challenging. Yet, prior research often fails to provide rigorous reasoning for their specific choices of loss, a fact the authors argue indicates a dogmatic approach in the deep learning community that overlooks the importance of empirical grounding. Addressing supervised classification in deep neural networks, this paper investigates how the selection of a particular loss function influences the outcomes of the model. Although certain standard losses may be suboptimal under optimal training strategies, empirical analysis within this work demonstrates that underestimated options such as Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence frequently surpass conventional top-tier choices with significant margins, underscoring that these components function as hyperparameters requiring careful tune-ability and careful consideration.

Effective Artificial Intelligence (AI) for analyzing document images typically relies on abundant labeled data, particularly for information extraction tasks. This study focuses on optimizing such AI performance when labeled data are sparse. We introduce a new refinement strategy that employs reinforcement learning: treating the Information Extraction model as a policy network, we utilize policy gradients to update parameters so as to maximize a combined reward that augments conventional cross-entropy losses rather than replacing them. Experiments across four diverse datasets, utilizing both standard labels and human feedback, indicate that our fine-tuning approach consistently enhances the capabilities of a leading Information Extraction system, yielding significant benefits specifically when only a minority of the training data are available.

When faced with algorithmic decision-makers, individuals strategically adjust their observable traits to maximize positive outcomes based on their assumptions. Since assessment rules are often deliberately hidden in real-world applications—to prevent strategy formation and preserve competitive edge—these individuals must operate with incomplete information when refining their traits. In this text-based framework, these interactions are modelled as a Bayesian persuader game where the system provides action recommendations to encourage beneficial modifications. Consequently, both the system and the user are expected at least to maintain parity, whereas the system may gain significant advantages mathematically. Although computing the optimal Bayesian Incentive-Compatible signaling strategy initially appears to involve infinite-variable optimization, we can reformulate this as a linear optimization problem across finitely defined regions of assessment rules. Following this, finding an efficient solution to the linearized problem requires managing an exponentially complex variable space, even for relatively simple instances, which motivated our creation of polynomial-time approximate schemes capable near-optimal signaling. Empirical evaluation through simulations of semi-synthetic data substantiate the advantages that persuasion strategies bring to Algorithmic recourse.

This paper proposes an automated approach for segmenting infection regions within lungs from CT scans of COVID-19 patients, offering quantitative diagnostic criteria that deliver both speed and accuracy. While prior methods utilizing either 2D slices or full 3D volumes struggle with variable infection sizes—frequently overlooking small areas—our Patch-based framework addresses this. To manage the inherent challenge in defining the appropriate patch size for detecting diverse infection scales, we exploit scale uncertainty across multiple receptive field sizes within a Segmentation Fully Convolutional Network (FCN), wherein receptive field dimensions equate to patch sizes and extraction resolutions. The proposed Infection Segmentation Network (ISNet) specializes in segmenting regions across varied intensity levels. To achieve this, we incorporate multiple encode path that processes volume patches normalized over diverse intensity ranges by collecting and fusing results from an ensemble of ISNets with distinct receptive field sizes using a scale-uncertainty-aware agglomeration strategy which produces refined segmentation outputs. Experimental validation on 199 chest CT volumes demonstrates that our aggregated prediction technique elevated the Dice Similarity Coefficient significantly from 47.6% to 62.1%.

The Smith chart acts as a critical instrument in analyzing measurements expressed through scattering parameters. By illustrating its fundamental definition alongside techniques for navigation within its boundaries, the discussion prepares the reader for practical use. Scholarly works on AI indicate that machine learning systems can detrimentally affect vulnerable social groups because biases inherent in the development process often result in policies and decisions that foster exclusion. Parallel to these challenges faced by diverse modern audiences, museums have undergone significant shifts in both theory and practice regarding how representation and meaning-making are constructed. Whereas early museology prioritized objects marked by grandeur and scarcity, contemporary practices now heavily integrate the consideration of folk life and the specific communities engaged with, aiming to improve accessibility and foster social inclusion by addressing these variances. Building upon this trajectory and drawing parallels from museum evolution to artificial intelligence, we posit that museums offer valuable insights for constructing AI systems with a focus on social inclusion, particularly when curation or filtering skills similar to those found in digital archives and search engines are required. We emphasize three core principles: firstly, rather than striving for claimed objectivity to neutralize their impact, professionals should recognize the influence of diverse perspectives—practicing cultural humility—to better identify and rectify existing flaws; secondly, interpretative nuance should persist beyond initial data gathering and model generation, ensuring that contextual realities are respected prior to applying predictions; and thirdly, engaging communities serves their direct interests while creating a meaningful bridge connecting stakeholders and creators alike.

Investigating collective phenomena demands manageable descriptions of correlations within assemblies of strongly interacting particles, with grasping their self-consistency being fundamental. The parquet approach achieves the highest degree of self-consistency possible for strictly two-particle many-body correlations. Although rooted in perturbation theory and based on an intricate system of nonlinear, strongly coupled integral equations for all-order scattering that are rigorously checked against physical crossings—and yet remains only heuristic—this core framework is explored here through Kraichnan's formalism applied to fermionic parquet structure using a Hamiltonian analysis. The form of its governing equations emerges directly from this canonical setup. We examine the resemblance between the scattering amplitude produced by a conservation-compliant form of this derived model and that of standard parquet theories: while this Hamiltonian model rigorously conserves microphysical quantities and fails to uphold crossing symmetry conversely, and conversely while parquet and similar variants maintain crossing symmetry and thus sacrifice micro-local conservation. The choice between these approaches relies not on theoretical purity but depends on whether specific physics requirements prioritize conserving interactions or maintaining crossing checks.

Recent advancements have demonstrated the benefit of integrating pre-trained models, such as BERT, into natural language processing (NLP) systems; however, these existing models currently lack the causal understanding required to emulate human reasoning. This paper explores the challenge of embedding causal knowledge into pre-trained architectures, focusing on two core issues: identifying diverse causal relations in arbitrary granularity from unstructured text, and devising an effective strategy to integrate these insights into models. We extend upon concepts derived from prior causal BERT research to address these challenges through experiments across various datasets, supplemented by a regularization method added as an extra constraint to retain the models' original knowledge while incorporating new causal information. The study, validated via extensive testing on seven different data types—including causal pair classification, question-answering, and inference tasks—confirms that our enhanced approach captures substantial causal understanding, surpasses all state-of-the-art BERT-based methods, and establishes a new record for causal inference performance.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator involves gap opening at the Fermi surface and is triggered by the spontaneous formation of electron-hole pairs through exciton condensation. While this theoretical concept has existed for generations, existing frameworks fall short, offering only qualitative explanations and lacking a tool for precise quantitative prediction. Addressing this shortfall, we introduced a method combining finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theories ($ab~initio$) specifically designed to analyze critical aspects of exciton condensation. Utilizing this approach on monolayer TiSe$_2$, we demonstrated that lattice distortion and excitonic gap generation result from electron-phonon coupling in the absence of phonon softening; consequently, exciton condensation confirms itself as the driving force behind the observed charge-density-wave state. This methodology is broadly applicable and establishes a foundation for future investigations into potential excitonic insulators within natural materials.

This work examines the interaction between off-shell and on-shell unfolded dynamics, introducing the formulation of invariant constraints required to transition an off-shell system onto the mass shell. This is achieved by incorporating new variables and derivatives within the target space, thereby enlarging the original $Q$-derivation of the unfolded formulation into a bicomplex structure. An analogy to the standard Euler-Lagrange equations is postulated for unfolded dynamics, while a generalized class of invariant constraints for equations of motion (on-shell equations) is characterized using cohomological language. A rigorous proof demonstrates that these on-shell constraints functionally serve as Euler-Lagrange equations if and only if specific necessary and sufficient conditions are met, a proposal that is substantiated by an illustrative case involving a scalar field.

Traditional structured prediction models typically aim to learn the conditional distribution, $p(y|x)$, representing the link between structured outputs $y$ and input features $x$. However, the likelihood computation is often non-computation feasible, making training difficulties; consequently, these approaches must rely on surrogate objectives or variational inference to approximate likelihood. In contrast, this paper introduces Conditional Glow (c-GLOW)—a conditional generative flow specifically designed for learning structured outputs—alongside the exact yet efficient generation capabilities of flow-based modeling for calculating $p(y|x)$, eliminating the need for proxies or inference steps during training. Moreover, after convergence, the model facilitates direct conditional sampling via a specialized sample-driven prediction method. Testing c-GLOW against various tasks yielded superior results compared to current state-of-the-art baselines on some datasets, while achieving on-par outputs on others. Collectively, these experimental outcomes demonstrate c-GLOW as a versatile framework applicable to numerous structured prediction scenarios.

Deep learning models frequently suffer significant performance drops when confronted with inputs atypical under their training distributions, such as those corrupted or shifted. Prior research indicates that adapting models at inference time (e.g., via entropy minimization) can effectively enhance performance in these scenarios beyond the training domain boundaries. This study addresses the setting of fully test-time adaptation, which requires solely unlabeled target-domain data to enable the robustness enhancement of arbitrary pre-trained backbones. We introduce an enhanced loss function designed to overcome common pitfalls in entropy minimization—namely, instability and premature convergence. By substituting entropy with a non-saturating surrogate and introducing a batch-level diversity regularizer, we actively prevent the model from collapsing into trivial low-entropy solutions. Furthermore, we integrate learnable input transformation layers preceding the network to counteract distributional shifts. Remarkably, this preprocessing module can be trained end-to-end via our adaptation objective in a fully unsupervised manner on target unlabeled data, without needing source data or target labels. Experimental results on ImageNet-C and other rigorous benchmarks confirm that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in bolstering the robustness of public image classification models against common data corruptions.

During analysis and numerical simulation, the particle's motion is reduced to calculating whether a specific two-dimensional potential possesses a negative local average.

We employed a first-principles density functional method to examine the electronic structure and magnetic anisotropy at the Fe/MgO interface, specifically in a magnetic metal/dielectric insulator system layered beneath a Cr film of low electronegativity. Results show that interface resonant states, contrary to the standard rigid band model, experience occupation by reduction in Fe layer thickness, correlating with significant thickness-dependent oscillatory patterns and large perpendicular anisotropies. Additionally, scenarios involving two-dimensional van Hove singularities arising from flat bands are analyzed, alongside an assessment of calculated anisotropy energy accuracies compared with existing experimental datasets.

Counting mitotic figures manually in the most active tumor zone is a fundamental metric for grading most cancers; however, this count varies significantly due to uneven mitotic distribution across the sample, depending heavily on the specific biopsy area chosen given the existing inter-rater inconsistency. This study assessed the impact of area selection by analyzing a set of 32 fully annotated H&E-stained whole slide images of canine cutaneous mast cell tumors. Eight veterinarians (including both board-certified experts and trainees) selected fields of interest for their counts, which we then compared against the slide's overall distribution. Additionally, the research evaluated three AI methodologies to identify regions of peak mitotic density: (1) a model performing regression directly on patch mitotic counts, (2) a method generating segmentation masks calculated for density, and (3) a two-stage object detector identifying specific figures using current-advance architectures. Results showed all algorithms averaged superior predictions to human expertise, with the two-stage detector outperming pathologist scores across most tumor samples and achieving the highest agreement with ground truth, ranging from 0.963 to 0.979 positional overlap, and variance was notably high.

Concepts within knowledge graphs (KGs) are crucial for enabling machine understanding of natural language and are vital to various applications. Network pruning offers a viable strategy for creating efficient yet accurate models designed for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. However, state-of-the-art methods currently assume a uniform distribution between effective sub-network parameters and redundancies, a simplification that inevitably truncations the underlying distribution. By indiscriminately eliminating values near zero—an ostensibly straightforward but often suboptimal approach—these methods ignore the reality that effective models frequently contain many naturally small values. Removing such intrinsic small parameters can drastically compromise accuracy. Furthermore, alternative approaches rely on assigning discrete priors to potential sub-structures based on manual design hypotheses, which are rarely ideal. Compounding these issues, existing techniques rely on hard pruning using point estimates and cannot generate error bounds, thereby undermining trustworthiness validation for the pruned networks. This study introduces DLLP, a distribution-lossless pruning method. Within a Bayesian framework, DLLP theoretically optimizes the "pruning lottery." Specifically, it models standard networks as discrete priors governing the latent pruned structure and its counterparts, specifically for the associated weight values. DLLP also employs Stein Variational Inference to estimate the latent prior without requiring the calculation of KL divergence involving known or easily computable unknown distributions, effectively bypassing traditional divergence estimation. Experimental evidence derived from small CIFAR-10 models and large-scale ImageNet datasets indicates that DLLP achieves significant network sparsity without sacrificing generalization, while additionally offering measurable reliability metrics for the final pruned architectures.

Using chest X-ray images for disease localization with a minimal amount of precise labeling significantly conserves manual efforts, although existing weakly-supervised techniques often produce incomplete or inaccurate localized regions. First, GREN employs a segmentation-pretrained U-Net to delineate lung lobes; it then models intra-lung relationships using an intra-image graph, while modeling inter-relationships via an inter-image graph built from the images within the same training batch, effectively emulating a radiologist's diagnostic process of scrutinizing multiple images and areas for consensus. To preserve critical structural information within the network's deep embedding layers for localization accuracy, we apply Hash coding and Hamming distance to construct these graphs for the purpose of graph-based structural regularization. Through this approach, we achieve state-of-the-art performance in weakly-supervised disease localization on the NIH chest X-ray dataset, with our source code available at (https://github.com/qibaolian/GREN).

We examine the modulational instability of Stokes waves—specifically small-amplitude, constant-speed, long-period gravity waves in both finite and infinite water depths. Utilizing a perturbation technique based on linearizing Euler's equations around these base states, we characterize the unstable spectral components of this instability with high precision. These components generate a characteristic "figure-eight” shape within the complex spectral plane, anchored at the origin and parameterized by a Floquet exponent. Our derived asymptotic formulas matching these loops align remarkably well with previous numerical simulations, theoretical rigorous findings by Berti, Maspero, and Ventura. Based on these high-order expansions, we calculate precise growth rates for the Benjamin-Feir effect and refine the parameterization relative to the exponent. Notably, for the first time, we provide an analytic comparison between Benjamin-Feir and high-frequency instability spectra, thereby defining three distinct regimes for Stokes wave stability determined by the prevailing instability mode.

Accurate Bird's Eye View (BEV) positioning and tracking of objects are crucial for perception applications such as interaction mapping and scenario analysis; however, acquiring the extensive 3D or annotated data typically needed to train systems for this task presents significant challenges. To address this, we introduce a lightweight, weakly supervised framework that simultaneously predicts 2D object bounding boxes and scene depth through a single network forward pass. Built upon a CNN-center-based one-shot detector, our model represents each object purely as BEV spatio-temporal points. Remarkably, it requires neither 3D nor BEV ground-truth labels during training nor employs point cloud queries during the inference stage. Our method utilizes standard 2D box annotations together with LiDAR point clouds (exclusive to the training phase) to teach a single network to handle detection and holistic depth estimation. This paper presents a general fault-tolerant protocol for quantum error correcting codes using flag circuits designed for stabilizer measurement across arbitrary distances. Sustaining continuous control and planning remains a significant obstacle in the fields of robotics and machine learning. We apply our technique to a sophisticated, real-world task prevalent in neuroscience, suggesting it serves as a robust basis for deciphering the neural and behavioral operations found in highly adaptive animal controller systems.

In this setup at DESY Hamburg, OLYMPUS quantified $e^-p$ and $e^+p$ elastic scattering by utilizing large-acceptance, toroidal magnetic spectroscopic to capture both scattered leptons and recoil protons. Engineered to precisely isolate TPE effects by measuring the $e^+/e^-\,cross$-section ratio, OLYMPUS verified its spectrometer absolute efficiencies through over-determined kinematics, enabling data extraction to cross-sections. Achieving loss compensation through gain insertion is a cornerstone in various fields, including photonics, nanophononics, and metamaterials. A notable advancement in this domain is found within parity-time (PT) symmetric structures, which maintain a balanced distribution between loss and gain. This research extends such phenomena to asymmetric configurations, demonstrating loss compensation in coupled multi-modal waveguide pairs with distinct radii containing both loss and gain dielectric components. We demonstrate that much like the PT-symmetric systems composed of single-mode wavegraphs with equal radii, these asymmetric arrangements feature "loss compensation (LC) thresholds" that mark an exceptional point; these are the frequencies at which the spectrum shifts from having complex to purely real values. Furthermore, enabling LC symmetry within asymmetric coupled modes of different types offers an expanded parameter space for controlling system dynamics. Specifically, as the loss and gain parameters within asymmetric coupled wavegraphs are varied, compensation across transverse magnetic (TM) and transverse electric (TE) configurations, as well as hybrid Heckman-Helfert (HE/ EH) configurations, becomes achievable.

This research is dedicated to investigating a more realistic setting capable of accommodating weakly-supervised, multi-modal instance-level product search within fine-grained categories. To facilitate experimental validation on retail price comparisons and personalized suggestion systems, we introduce the Product1M dataset and formally define two practical tasks. **Significance**: Monte Carlo Ray Tracking (MCRT) represents the premier standard for simulating photon propagation within turbid environments. Conventional MCRT implementations generally rely on voxels or meshes to simulate physical structures, a discretized nature that prevents the faithful representation of smooth, continuous surfaces characteristic of biological tissues or food container materials.

**Aim**: We introduce **sMCRT** (or signedMCRT), a new geometry-aware algorithm that utilizes Signed Distance Functions (SDF) for geometric representation, a technique enabling precise modeling of curved geometries alongside intricate structures.

**Approach**: Employing SDF-based geometry demonstrates greater precision and computational efficiency compared to voxel methods. The sMCRT framework is designed to seamlessly retrofit into established voxel-based Monte Carlo systems.

**Results**: Validation exercises confirm the accuracy of the sMCRT approach against theoretical standards, existing voxel codes, and complex applications like modeling dense microvascular networks using SDFs; notably, the sMCRT delivers up to 45-fold accuracy gains for curved surface problems compared to state-of-the-art alternative methods.

**Conclusions**: By achieving high-speed performance (up to 45 times more accurate and 4-6 times faster for comparable scenarios) and superior handling of curved topologies, the sMCRT framework surpasses current voxel models in precision. The source code is released publicly via the repository at https://github.com/lewisfish/signedMCRT.

This paper offers a holistic examination of experimental design applications within surrogate modeling, specifically highlighting the critical role these designs play in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), a category of supervised learning. Relying on machine learning (ML) models for high-stakes decisions poses significant risks because, despite their output, humans ultimately bear the accountability for these choices rather than machines itself. Machine Learning Explainability (MLX) offers a solution by delivering decision-specific justifications that reassure stakeholders of both the reliability of predictions and the validity of the underlying logic. However, most existing research fails to explicitly address this vital "human-in-the-loop" (HITL) responsibility gap.

To bridge this gap, this work introduces HEX, a deep reinforcement learning framework tailored for MITL explainability. Unlike previous approaches, it uses "zero-thust trust projection" to create policies tailored by the specific human decider for explanations derived from any base classification model. Furthermore, the system is designed to function effectively under low-data conditions, including those found in federated learning. Rather than depending solely on the original training datasets—a common weakness in agnostic MLX methods—our formulation explicitly models the decision boundaries of target machine learning systems. Consequently, the proposed approach generates HITL explainability policies specifically adapted to the decision boundaries of relevant models for operation in rare data scenarios.

Cellular automata (CA) are known for their ability to generate intricate behaviors arising from simple localized interactions. Although some aspects of these traits have already influenced meta-heuristics for global optimization, the evolution rules specific to CA remain underutilized for optimizing purposes. Motivated by the diverse complexities introduced by various CA evolution rules, researchers have proposed a new method: the Continuous-state Cellular Automata Algorithm (CCAA). This algorithm leverages distinct rules to sustain equilibrium between exploitation and exploration properties during each iteration. CCAA's efficacy was validated using 33 benchmark test cases standard in literature, four engineering problems previously addressed in recent studies, and the design of adaptive infinite-impulse response (IIR) filters evaluated via 10 full-order IIR functions. Numerical data confirm its competitiveness against state-of-the-art techniques, and the corresponding CCAA source code can be freely retrieved from https://github.com/juanseck/CCAA.git.

Explanations for automated recommendation have emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing system persuasiveness, user satisfaction, and transparency. A central challenge in this field, however, remains how to effectively evaluate the generated explanations. Although the last decade has seen numerous proposals addressing this, the strategies remain fragmented without a unified systematic comparison. Our goal is to address this gap through a thorough review and the introduction of distinct taxonomies organized by both evaluation perspectives and techniques. We do more than summarize existing approaches; we also critically analyze the pros and cons of these methods and outline a series of practical guidelines for their selection. Building upon an extensive survey of over 100 seminal publications from top venues such as *IJCAI*, *AAAI*, *RecSys*, and others—including our complete summary on Shimo.im—this work aims to offer a definitive and all-encompassing comprehensive review on evaluating recommendations with explanations.

The expanding presence of Electric Vehicles (EVs) triggers multiple impacts, spanning from lowered greenhouse gas emissions and localized pollution shifts to altered traffic patterns and electricity demand. Notably, the operational decisions within the transportation and electrical sectors become intertwined because each is influenced by EV behavior. Consequently, effective decision-making demands a complex modeling framework involving several interdependent operators alongside diverse EV driving and charging habits. The authors propose such a trilevel-structured model specifically for commuter scenarios within the power sector. At the bottom tier, congestion game mechanics allow commuters to select driving routes and charging hubs based on travel time duration and associated consumption expenses. The middle level involves a Charging Service Provider determining hub pricing strategies aimed at optimizing the margin between revenue earned from charging and supply costs for electricity, the rates for which are dictated by the upper-level Electrical Network Operator. The highest level focuses on the Network Operator's objective to minimize overall grid costs. This trilevel optimization challenge is addressed implementing an optimistic iterative bilateral algorithm integrated with simulated annealing. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the proposed model regarding external parameters—specifically EV adoption rates and potential incentives from transportation authorities—is demonstrated through case studies on authentic urban networks.

Determining whether stars in the Milky Way were formed in situ or accreted remains a intricate and challenging task. Leveraging Gaia kinematics alongside APOGEE elemental abundance data, we isolated members of the Gaia-Saurus-Enceladus (GSE) and Sequoia accretion events to analyze their metallicity distribution functions, element abundance signatures, age distributions, and the mass distributions of their progenitor galaxies. Our results indicate the GSE group has a mean metallicity ([Fe/H]) of approximately -1.15 and an average age between 10-12 billion years; its stars follow a single track on the [Mg/Fe] versus [Fe/H] diagram that marks the introduction of Iron from Ia-type supernovae and maintain consistently low [Al/Fe] levels near -0.25 dex. In contrast, characterizations of the Sequoia group vary significantly depending on kinematic criteria used; utilizing a non-contaminating selection where $J_{\phi}/J_{\mbox{tot}} < -0.6$ offers optimal results. This specific filter identifies a mean metallicity for Sequoia around -1.3, with an average age spanning 12-14 Gyr, marked by a complex abundance mix dominated by stars high in magnesium ([Mg/Fe]). Finally, we utilize the GSE aluminum versus magnesium relationship to establish a chemically-driven purification process, effectively filtering contaminant stars from these accreted populations.

Active learning strives to create algorithms that are efficient with labels by identifying and querying the most representative data points for human annotation. Our architecture pairs a feature encoding network that minimizes entropy with a classification layer that maximizes it via a discriminator also engaged in minimax optimization. This formulation seeks to narrow the distributional gap between labeled and unlabeled datasets while allowing the trained discriminator to classify these groups. Samples selected for annotation are those exhibiting maximum predicted entropy from the classifier yet flagged by the discriminator as coming from the unlabeled population. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets for image classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate performance that surpasses current state-of-the-art methodologies.

Computational modeling has emerged as a vital instrument in quantitative sciences for deciphering how intricate systems evolve temporally. However, these models often feature a vast array of unconstrained parameters that cannot be derived theoretically and instead require inference from empirical data; this demand is particularly prevalent in social sciences, economics, and computational epidemiology. Many existing estimation techniques are mathematically complex and computationally prohibitive in this context. This paper proposes a fast, simple approach to accurately recover the probability densities of model parameters via neural differential equations. The method integrates multi-agent models—which function as forward solvers for systems of ordinary or stochastic differential equations— with a neural network designed to pinpoint parameters within data generated by these agents. This combined architecture offers an efficient means to rapidly estimate parameter distributions, even for extremely large systems. The method is illustrated through synthetic time-series generated by the infection-spreading SIR model and applied, along with a thorough analysis of the non-convex Harris-Wilson economic network activity model, using both simulated data and real-world economic data for London. For this latter application, our approach calibrates the Harris-Wilson model significantly more accurately than previous classical studies of the same dataset, while executing 195 to 390 times faster.

To drastically decrease the significant computational costs of time-domain simulations, this article presents a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) designed to learn the solutions governing power system dynamics directly. Addressing the limitations typical of classical model order reduction methods used to speed up simulations, PINNs are capable of universally approximating any continuous function with high precision across various scales. A novel aspect of this work is that it eliminates the requirement for empirical training data by embedding the underlying differential equations along with an implicit Runge-Kutta integration scheme directly into the network's learning phase. This strategy enables the prediction of dynamical power system trajectories at any discrete time step. Consequently, these resulting physics-informed Runge-Kutta neural networks (RK-PINNs) can compute dynamic evaluations up to a hundred times faster than standard time-domain simulations. Implemented on a single-machine infinite bus system governed by the swing equation, we verify that RK-PINNs deliver solutions both quickly and accurately.

This research introduces a compact, non-linear, recursive filter based on Gauss-Newton principles—a method grounded in weighted least squares with local linear optimization via Newton's approach. Adapted from a weighted form (RGNF) using the Levenberg-Marquardt scheme, this filter effectively manages state models that are both linear and nonlinear alongside compatible observation schemes. Simulation tests verify the robustness of the RGNF and highlight its capability for significantly reducing computational memory usage, which was previously a key barrier in the application and adoption of Gauss-Newton.

To explore song evolution between 1960 and 2010, we analyzed the complexity of thousands of audio recordings from the Million Song Dataset by examining pitch, loudness, timbre, and rhythm. Comparing popular songs to random selections reveals a tight clustering of complex measures around an average, which aligns with the notion of an inverted U-curve relating complexity to perceived pleasure. Our longitudinal analysis identifies consistent shifts across the decades: average loudness complexity declined from its mid-century high point, while timbre complexity generally rose despite stability in popular songs alone. Contradicting assertions that modern hits sound increasingly similar, we find no greater pitch or rhythmic uniformity today compared to fifty years prior; nonetheless, timbral trends differ distinctly by era, and loudness complexity continues to grow. Lastly, these specific complexity signatures enable the differentiation of musical genres.

This letter initiates a probe of detectable dark sector phenomena stemming from binary neutron star mergers (BNSs), specifically targeting dark photon emissions occurring within 1 milliseconds to 1 second of the coalescence. We demonstrate that these emissions can generate conspicuous, short-lived gamma-ray transients. Characterised by approximate isotropy, these signals frequently exhibit nearly thermal properties with an estimated temperature near 100 keV. Notably for much of the relevant parameter space, these attributes distinguish them from standard short-duration gamma bursts associated with BNSs, which are distinctively beamed and non-thermal in nature. We quantify the expected signal intensity and establish that masses in the range of 1–100 MeV can readily yield total luminosities exceeding 10$^{46}$ erg s$^{-1}$ across a broad and largely unconstrained portion of the parameter space. Furthermore, this detectable signature provides access to a substantial volume of the parameter space encouraged by freeze-in dark matter frameworks mediated via dark photons at these energy scales, and we conclude by outlining anticipated methodologies for enhanced sensitivity from forthcoming observatories in gravity and electromagnetic mid-band detection.

We present an original asymmetric plasmonic-photonic hybrid system designed to perform all-optical switching and readout for ferrimagnetic bit media. Effectively bridging this gap between nanomagnetic spin systems and integrated optics, the technology accelerates the realization of highly rapid, power-dissipation minimization for future on-chip functionalities.

Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) seeks to derive nearly optimal policies using incomplete datasets gathered beforehand, avoiding further engagement with the environment. Their synergy significantly boosts both the effectiveness and adaptive range of offline RL agents. Evaluated against the D4RL benchmark, MABE delivers higher average results than established prior arts, both for model-free and model-based methods across numerous research settings. Furthermore, scenarios testing the ability to adapt between domains show MABe consistently surpassing existing methodologies. When applied to Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), deep learning typically involves training classification models with 2D slices from volumetric scans. However, due to the micron-scale resolution inherent to OCT systems, successive images exhibit high similarity between structural patterns and noise, often leading to an inappropriate data split that creates unwanted overlap between testing and training sets—a critical issue frequently ignored in current literature. To investigate the consequences, we analyzed the performance impact on three distinct classification scenarios using well-established public repositories: Kermany's SDR and Srinivasan datasets from ophthalmology, and the breast imaging dataset from AIIMS, along with other standard resources, to evaluate how faulty splitting practices inflate model performance metrics and generate erroneous benchmarks.

Research linking epidemiology and genetics within chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and various complex conditions indicates subgroup differences, such as those defined by sex. This work approaches the challenge through integrative analysis, merging diverse data sources including clinical, genotypic, and proteomic information. Current methods fail to account for subgroup-based heterogeneity, whereas combining data views to handle such heterogeneity precludes modeling relationships between these views. To resolve these issues, we introduce a statistical framework for joint association modeling and prediction; by combining data views efficiently, our method detects both shared sex-specific molecular signatures and unique contributors to the variation of COPD, quantifying via airway wall thickness. This framework, named Heterogeneity in Integration and Prediction (HIP), accommodates sex-specific variation to maintain subgroup characteristics, utilizes sparsity in regulatory network variable selection, adapts to multiclass scenarios alongside univariate/multivariate outputs, and supports adjustment using covariates. Efficient algorithms for HIP are provided within the PyTorch ecosystem, facilitating streamlined application in modeling. Based on the application to COPD, our studies have highlighted several proteins, gene sets, and corresponding pathways that are either common or sex-specific in male patients compared to females; notably, these discoveries include established contributors to COPD, as well as potentially yielding fundamental understanding of the molecular drivers behind sex differences in this condition.

Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) serves as an advanced technique for learning from expert demonstrations; this work specifically targets IRL tasks where we have prior assurance that optimal policies will respect certain constraints. Standard methods, which overlook these restrictions, typically require extensive data to converge. To address this, we introduce Xor-Maximum Entropy Constrained Inverse Reinforcement Learning (X-MEN), a method guaranteed to reach the optimal policy linearly regarding the number of iterations. X-MEN integrates XOR-sampling—an efficient approach converting #P-complete tasks into NP oracle queries—within the Maximum Entropy IRL framework, ensuring the resulting policy strictly never produces trajectories violating the constraints. Navigation experiments confirm X-MEN's superiority over baseline algorithms by both accelerating convergence to optimal policies and successfully generating trajectories compliant with complex, multi-state combinatorial requirements.

While profile-guided optimization (PGO) significantly boosts compiler performance through dynamic behavioral data, gathering that profile information can be costly, difficult, and necessitates frequent updates for accuracy. To address this, we introduce an innovative statistical model designed to estimate branch probabilities, thereby enhancing program performance on compilable code that lacks PGO. By performing offline training against a vast collection of binaries known for their branch probability data, we create a learned model. Compiler developers can then utilize this tool to anticipate the branch behavior of standard, uninstrumented code, allowing the compiler to refine its optimizations accordingly. Our implementation is fully woven into LLVM, acting as an additive enhancement to existing manual compiler heuristics. Performance testing across various benchmarks shows measurable improvements compared to compilations run without any profiling insights not present in PGO. In a production context, our approach eliminates the need for separate profiling runs while incurring only minimal overhead during the compilation process.

This research introduces a simulation-driven framework designed to optimize and calibrate dynamic travel demand models at a municipal scale for real-time applications, emphasizing high-level disaggregated microsimulations in congested environments. The core calibration method incorporates sequential optimization for demand estimation within brief intervals, utilizing continuous streams of vehicle flow data collected by IoT sensors. Building off standard bi-level optimization structures, the approach formulates the upper-level challenge as a bounded variable quadratic programming model for each time slice to achieve computational feasibility. During these intervals, the probabilistic variables of route-choice models evolve through an iterative feedback process connecting the origin-destination optimization layer (upper level) with stochastic dynamic traffic assignment via parallel simulation samples (lower level). Critically, the network's microsimulated state carries over from one interval to the next to maintain temporal dependency and continuity. Furthermore, convergence speeds are enhanced by applying the fixed-point technique to update segment travel times. This sequential model offers substantial computational savings over existing solutions by dividing operations into short segments and relying only on historical and contemporary demand data, thereby eliminating the need for prior reliable population estimates. Given its ability to ingest real-time field measurements and its high algorithmic efficiency per interval, the framework effectively addresses the complexities of high-dimensional online and real-time applications. The authors validated the approach using both synthesized datasets and the Tartu city network in Estonia, demonstrating high accuracy even when operating under stringent resource limits.

X-ray emissions originating from the surfaces of isolated neutron stars (NSs) are frequently detected across various sources, exhibiting universal pulsations that imply heat arises either from localized regions heated by external processes, the whole cooling surface with non-uniform temperatures, or both. Because heat transport within an NS's crust predominantly occurs along magnetic field lines, the resulting thermal landscape aligns with the magnetic field topology. Therefore, self-consistent surface thermal distributions emerge naturally by simulating a star where magnetic field and thermal evolution evolve simultaneously. We modeled the three-dimensional thermal evolution of an NS crust using distinct initial magnetic field configurations, subsequently utilizing the resulting thermal maps to predict the observable spectral features, pulse profiles (from an observer at infinity), and accounting for general relativistic corrections. Generally, models exhibiting a high degree of symmetry (such as those without additional quadrupoles beyond a primary dipole) yield minimal pulsed fractions ($\lesssim 5\%$). In contrast, inherently three-dimensional scenarios—created by introducing a quadrupole component into the initial dipolar field—result in more complex field structures and significantly larger pulsed fractions, reaching up to approximately $25\%$. Constructing query graphs involves transforming natural language questions into valid, executable SPARQL statements for Knowledge Graph inference. While contemporary neural ranking approaches yield promising results, tackling intricate question types introduces three primary hurdles: complex SPARQL syntax, an expanded search domain, and local ambiguities within query graphs. We address this with a targeted framework. Initially, we model SPARQL clauses as vertex-edge subgraphs and introduce a Unified Graph Grammar termed AQG to formalize graph structures. Leaning on these components, we develop an end-to-end framework that employs hierarchical autoregressive decoding for sequence generation. High-level decoding constructs an AQG that serves as a mechanism to narrow the search namespace and eliminate local ambiguity in query graphs; conversely, low-level decoding assembles specific instances from candidate pools to occupy AQG slots. Empirical evaluations demonstrate substantial gains over state-of-the-art techniques on datasets featuring complex Knowledge Graph QA tasks, and integration with pre-trained language models pushes the state of the art across all evaluated datasets.

The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) has caused Radio Frequency (RF) channels to become increasingly crowded with diverse communication demands from new devices. Addressing this congestion requires technological advancements to (i) maximize bit rates within restricted bandwidth limits, (ii) coexist seamlessly with established RF protocols, and (iii) adapt dynamically to the evolving landscape of digital communications. To this end, we introduce methods utilizing deep neural networks for spectral filling. By operating alongside a channel transmitting pre-modulated information without causing interference, our approach automatically constructs new signal components that convey additional data in conjunction with the primary messages, thereby boosting total capacity without expanding spectrum usage. We also showcase how these signals can closely mirror original modulation patterns, rendering embedded information undetectable to external observers. Our study presents three computational validations and concludes with a discussion regarding the significance of these findings for contemporary RF applications.

A prevalent belief among the general public posits that cellular network densification—the large-scale placement of base stations—invariably causes an unchecked, exponential surge in radio frequency "pollution" affecting human exposure. To render this concept accessible, this study introduces a straightforward computational model for radio frequency "pollution" derived from a series of conservative, worst-case premises. The paper subsequently offers analytical formulas to assess the flux of radio frequency "pollution" across two proposed 5G deployment strategies under varying levels of density. By examining a broad array of typical 5G configurations, these findings dismantle misconceptions: when radiated transmission power is scaled to meet a baseline minimum cell-edge sensitivity, cellular intensification actually reduces exposure to radio frequency "pollution" by up to three orders of magnitude, thereby disproving the notion of uncontrolled pollution levels; we also identify specific conditions where exposure might rise—specifically if transmission power failure to scale inversely with cell reduction—but affirm that it remains invariably bounded. The study concludes with simulation outcomes that validate both scenarios, aligning with the proposed modeling predictions.

This study investigates how cryogenically cooling a Ti:sapphire laser crystal diminishes thermal lensing effects by a factor greater than ten, attributable to dual mechanisms: a surge in thermal conductivity and a reduced dependence of refractive index on temperature. Cavity stability analysis indicates that maintaining an anamorphic ratio between horizontal and vertical optimal cavity lengths below 0.1% requires the thermal lens focal length to exceed 0.5 meters when operating under pump conditions generating 100 W of output power—specifically achievable via cooling the crystal below 100 K. Consequently, single-crystal Ti:sapphire systems cooled to cryogenic temperatures are highly poised to deliver 100 W output power through this thermal management strategy.

Traditional unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) models typically require joint access for training to both labeled source and unlabeled target data. However, in many situations, source samples are withheld due to privacy or security concerns. To address this need, source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) has emerged as a focal point for researchers, providing only a pre-trained source model and unlabeled target data. Current SFDA approaches primarily rely on pseudo-labeling techniques or data generation; yet, they often fail to explicitly minimize distribution discrepancies—the critical factor for successful domain adaptation. We have observed that despite the unavailability of direct source samples, certain target instances are highly representative of the source domain, effectively serving as a "pseudo-source" approximation. Inspired by this insight, we introduce a novel method that leverages this pseudo-source concept by first synthesizing and expending the approximated data. Subsequently, we utilize four distinct loss functions grounded in a pseudo-labeling framework to align the distribution of this pseudo-source with the true source. Notably, a domain adversarial loss is implemented to bridge the gap between this pseudo-source subset and the remainder of the target dataset, specifically targeting a significant reduction in domain shift. Experiments across three real-world benchmarks confirm the efficacy of our proposed approach.

Furthermore, dEs in the cluster's periphery exhibit marginally steeper CMRs than their inner cluster counterparts, likely attributed to a population of low-luminosity, blue dEs in the outer regions by fitting these data with luminosity-dependent delayed exponential star formation models. These observations reinforce that delayed star formation in Virgo's early-type dwarfs correlates significantly with morphology and environmental context. Specifically, dS0 CMRs align with models involving considerable delays. These findings imply that dS0s represent transitional objects where late-type progenitors are evolving into standard, reddish dEs under the influence of cluster environments. Robust Markov decision processes (MDPs), or RMDPs, are a cornerstone of research in dynamic optimization under uncertainty and have generated significant inquiry. Although core MDP concepts, including value and policy iteration algorithms, extend naturally to RMDPs, a convex optimization framework akin to standard MDPs has remained unknown. This study introduces the first convex optimization model for RMDPs assuming sa- and s-rectangularity. By employing exponential variable substitution and entropic regularization, we develop this formulation, which features a linear scale of variables and constraints, albeit with substantial coefficients. Integrating proven efficient convex optimization methods enables the creation of new algorithms to solve RMDPs under uncertain probability distributions. We additionally simplify this approach for scenarios involving polyhedral uncertainty sets. Ultimately, this work initiates a fresh research avenue for RMDPs and provides a crucial initial step toward a tractable, fully convex representation of these models.

We present a method for realizing homogeneous atom-cavity interaction by filtering for $^{87}$Rb atoms positioned to couple maximally to the cavity's standing-wave mode. This selection is achieved by applying an AC Stark shift on the hyperfine ground-state microwave transition via light coupled into the cavity; consequently, atoms strongly coupled become resonant with applied microwaves to induce a spin flip. Finally, we eliminate the cavity entirely from atoms in the original spin state using radiation pressure forces, while retained atoms exhibit the desired high coupling uniformity. Improved homogeneity in the atom-cavity system holds the potential to advance entanglement generation, intracavity driving of atomic levels, cavity-optomechanics, and quantum simulations. Furthermore, this technique is straightforward to adapt to different atomic species, leveraging either microwave or optical transitions.

While pre-trained language models have advanced significantly in dialogue handling, relying on surface-level text typically limits their grasp of the core semantic essence of conversational contexts. We explore Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR), utilizing this explicit semantic framework to bolster model pre-training for better extraction of key dialogue information during the learning process. We introduce an AMR-driven pre-training system that augments the standard approach (Devlin et al., 2019) through three specific tasks designed to master 1) fundamental semantic units, 2) inter-semantic connections via AMR graphs, and 3) holistic semantic structures. Empirical evaluations on various tasks, ranging from casual chits to complex goal-directed conversations, highlight the model's effectiveness. To date, this study appears to be the inaugural effort to integrate such profound semantic representations explicitly into pre-training for dialogues.

The emergence of deep learning and expansive autonomous driving datasets has propelled univocular 3D object detection (Uni3D) to unprecedented heights. Nonetheless, the application of these models in practice faces a severe, underexplored obstacle during transfer between different domains, primarily due to label scarcity in target environments. This study systematically examines the core cause of this domain shift in Uni3D: geometric misalignment between source and target data that triggers a depth-shift problem. Addressing this, we present STMono3D, a self-learning framework designed specifically for unsupervised domain adaptation in Unary3D tasks. Our approach combats the depth-shift through an anatomy-constrained, multi-range training regime that decouples camera intrinsic parameters and enforces geometric alignment. Leveraging this, we construct a professor-mentee paradigm using a novel architecture to produce context-specific false annotations that optimize training on the target dataset. Our end-to-end method, which utilizes these annotations to convey detailed object quality cues through pseudo-confidence scores, includes an awareness mechanism ensuring more efficient training. It also incorporates positive mining strategies alongside dynamic threshold adjustments to effectively mitigate the issues of excessive false negatives and false positives caused by imperfect supervision. Experimental results show that STMono3D significantly improves task accuracy across various benchmarks, overtaking even fully supervised methods on the KITTI dataset for 3D object localization. This work notably pioneers techniques to explore effective unsupervised domain adaption in Unary3D applications.

Conclusive evidence suggests iCANS will be valuable in actualizing VHQCAs, specifically under the constraints of realistic measurement limits.

Active Learning (AL) strategies seek to reduce the human labeling effort by minimizing the training dataset needed for a specific model. In pool-based AL, the process begins with an initial labeled set from which informative samples are iteratively selected for annotation, often starting with a randomly drawn group. Despite growing focus on query function robustness in recent studies, the impact of how the initial labeled pool is constructed in deep active learning has been largely overlooked. Motivated by advancements in self-supervised and unsupervised representation learning, we explore whether an intelligently constructed initial seed set enhances performance. Our investigation employs both self-supervised and unssupervised techniques for pool selection and explicitly details the peer-review validation process undertaken before experimentation. Results indicated that, in the long run, intelligently designed seed sets do not definitively outperform random selection, though a Variational Autoencoder-based approach exhibited promising trends warranting further research.

While generative models defined on joint distributions of sentence-parse pairs offer benefits for parsing and language modeling, they constrain the available features and typically lag behind discriminative alternatives. To address these issues, we introduce an encoding-decoding architecture that combines a generative model with discriminative recognition, creating a unified framework for both tasks. Supported by mathematical justifications from variational inference and expectation maximization, this approach demonstrates the ability to achieve effective parsing and language modeling within a single implementation. Evaluations on the English Penn Treebank reveal that the model achieves state-of-the-art results in language modeling while reaching competitive levels on constituency parsing.

This work introduces an implicit-explicit finite volume method for the Euler equations. The numerical procedure divides this into two parts: an explicit component, utilizing a Godunov-type scheme built on a simplified Riemann solver to handle the acoustic portion, and an implicit component, involved in resolving elliptic equations for the fast acoustic pressure while projecting relaxation source terms to the equilibrium manifold via solution projections. The presented scheme guarantees the non-negativity of density and internal energy, and serves to remain robust and converge asymptotically to the Euler insystem as desired limits. For the constructed, consistent first order approach we derive a corresponding second extension that maintains positive characteristic value approximations of density internal and energy. Conducting 2 dimensional 2 and number-one 3-D computations we show the potential use case of the splitting method along with results about the convergence speed.

Learning models equipped with superior generalization to unseen fields, particularly in computer vision scenarios where labeled training data for the target domain is missing, is critical. This approach proves highly versatile, applicable to a wide array of sources and offering significant value for real-world usage. To address this, we introduce the "Domain-Awaited Meta-Symmetry-Analysis" (Domain-Awaited) protocol designed to construct generalizable, open-domain feature embeddings by introducing two augmentation strategies: (1) a novel technique at level-x using a new Distribution-mixing method (Dir), which fills in missing class representations and extends existing domain knowledge; and (2) a strategy at label level-x using the distilled method (Dist), which complements these gaps effectively. We execute meta-learning tasks optimized over cross-sections (sections/designs) through the modification and application (loss-weighting) which balances preservation with preservation and balances preservation with generalizability. As shown in results with a range of datasets, our approach ("Domain-Awaited Meta-Symmetry-Analysis") achieves greater superiority (meta-performer/advancement) in identifying unseen sections when evaluated against state-of-the-art methods.

Variation in renewable energy supply creates disruptions spanning from power grids into natural gas networks; to safeguard sector integrity, gas network managers must often revise supply targets, a process that entails high costs. This cost is alleviated by formulating control strategies utilizing the flexibility inherent in linepack—gas retained within pipe conductors—to counterbalance stochastic extraction demands. Built upon a finite discrete horizon of multi-stage linear inference rules, our methodology guides adjustable assets, such as valve and compressor units, into feasible operational modes with optimal efficiency. This approach provides versatile applications within network administration: initially by leveraging stored gas volume to absorb power grid disturbances while preserving nominal supply schedules; secondly, through optimization techniques aimed at minimizing variability stemming from renewable intermittency and variance arising from unpredictability, specifically regarding network state variables like pressure levels; and finally, through enabling strategic re-arrangement and configuration to segment the network architecture effectively, thereby hindering uncertainty spread throughout. Practical effectiveness illustrated through simulation-based numbers corroborate these results.

We introduce an ideal model where an intelligent forager can search for food across a larger spatial range. This agent adopts ballistic motion directed toward closest food only when that prey falls within its detection radius ($R$); when prey lies beyond this radius, it diffuses randomly because of the extended search range. However, increased intelligence raises the metabolic cost of movement. Consequently, low-intelligence foragers meander blindly at low cost but are prone to missing accessible food and starving, while high-intelligence foragers face high movement expenses due to constant precise tracking and also become starvation-prone. We demonstrate that the maximum lifespan for an intelligent forager is achieved by maintaining an optimal, intermediate intelligence level, balancing detection efficiency with metabolic expenditure.

Coupled-cluster theory including single and double excitations (CCSD) represents a viable *ab initio* approach for modeling electronic structures in three-dimensional metals, where second-order perturbation theory (MP2) typically diverges as the system approaches the thermodynamic limit. When combined, the methods allow for the estimation of CCSD correlation energy at full convergence, revealing that CCSD recaptures over 90% of exact correlation energy at an $r_s$ of 4. This study investigates the potential of both enhancing and efficiently integrating recurrent structures within Transformer architectures through the development of a highly rudimentary module. Satisfying the requirement for transporting gas centrally, which drives the high luminosity of an active galactic nucleus (AGN), is a necessary condition. These conflicts may arise from disparities in the spatial and temporal scales governing gas inflow, black-hole accretion, and emission, but sample selection biases could also be responsible; both identifying bar structures and characterizing AGN activity depend heavily on specific methodological choices. By analyzing data from SDSS, the authors revisit the connection between bars and AGN activity using emission-line diagnostics to confirm AGN status and the software package \texttt{BUDDA}, utilized previously for 2D decomposing bulges, bar structures. A core difficulty in millimeter wave (mmWave) communications is their vulnerability to physical obstacles, which compromise link availability and overall network service quality. Addressing this complex optimization task, we propose a low-complexity algorithm derived from stochastic block gradient descent; this approach efficiently estimates blockage patterns without exhaustively evaluating all possible blocked-link combinations. Numerical analyses demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly improves performance metrics regarding outage probability and achievable effective data rate compared to baseline methods.

Estimating prediction confidence seeks to measure model reliability, thereby offering insights into expected performance accuracy. In ideal real-world scenarios involving noisy data or out-of-distribution inputs, well-calibrated confidence scores are crucial for anticipating failures and accurately gauging risk. Despite this utility, the task proves significantly difficult within neural machine translation (NMT), where standard soft softmax probabilities fail to indicate when the model has erred effectively.

To overcome these limitations, this work introduces an unsupervised, jointly trained framework that generates confidence estimates alongside the NMT process itself. We define confidence as the quantity of auxiliary hints required for the model to achieve a correct translation: a higher need for hints corresponds to lower confidence. Under this framework, the model is empowered to request hints to enhance translation precision at the cost of a minimal penalty, and its reliability is approximated by tallying the number of requested hints. Our findings indicate that this learned confidence metric yields superior results in comprehensive sentence- and word-level quality assessments. Furthermore, analytical evaluations demonstrate its efficacy in assessing underlying risk across two practical applications: identifying contaminated data and recognizing out-of-domain sources. Additionally, we introduce a novel confidence-driven, instance-specific label smoothing technique grounded in our confidence estimates, which yields improved outcomes compared to conventional label smoothing.

Although vital for finance, the computational complexity of traditional mean-variance portfolio optimization prompts financial institutions to rely on slow approximate methods. While formulating this problem as linear equations allows for theoretical speedup via the HHL quantum algorithm, significant hurdles remain due to incompatibilities between HHL stages and current Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. To bridge this gap, this study introduces "NISQ-HHL," the first hybrid algorithm enabling complete small-scale portfolio optimization execution on NISQ systems. NISQ-HHL builds upon existing hybrid versions by incorporating modern device capabilities such as mid-circuit measurement, bit reuse and resetting, Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL), and a novel strategy for optimizing Hamiltonian simulation time. Crucially, it marks the first deployment of QCL-enhanced Phase Estimation on real trapped-ion infrastructure, specifically the Quantinuum H1-1 system. Although demonstrated within finance, the scalability methods developed for HHL through NISQ-HHL hold broad applicability for diverse solvable problems throughout the era of NISQ computing.

Smart speakers are becoming increasingly popular, yet they pose significant privacy risks whenever wake-up words trigger accidentally, resulting in unauthorized recording. While built-in designs offer controls such as mute switches, research suggests these mechanisms are infrequently utilized. To address this, we introduce the Privacy Hat: a physical accessory designed to sit on smart speaker hardware and disable its microphone based on input from focus groups and a functional prototype created as a result. We propose that the tactile and physical nature of using the Hat makes the concept of privacy control more accessible, thereby encouraging users to actively engage in privacy-protecting actions like muting the device. Additionally, we view the Privacy Hat as a valuable instrument for self-observation, assuming the object facilitates reflection on usage habits. Below, we outline the device concept, present the prototype details, and share our preliminary findings.

The analysis of one-shot devices represents an extreme instance of interval censoring, as failure occurrence can only be classified as happening before or after the test time. Certain types of these non-failure-inducing devices can survive testing, offering valuable inference regarding survival prior to inspections. Their reliability can be swiftly estimated through Accelerated Life Tests (ALTs) conducted under escalated stress conditions beyond normal operation, particularly using step-stress methods where the test progression allows for gradual, predefined stress increases over time. Typically, step-stress frameworks assume the cumulative exposure model, which connects a unit's lifetime distribution at any given stress level to those from previous, preceding levels. This study constructs robust estimators and Z-statistic tests grounded in density power divergence (DPD), designed to assess linear null hypotheses for the exponential lifetime distribution of non-destroyed one-shot devices subjected to step-stress ALTs. Investigating the asymptotic and robustness characteristics of these methods yields precision points and confidence intervals for key reliability metrics, including the mean and various distribution quantiles. Finally, we evaluate the performance of these inferential approaches through a computer-based simulation and apply the methods to illustrate their utility using actual real-world data.

Just as with other physical instruments, hyperspectral cameras generate various types of noise within the acquired datasets, making the denoising process a vital prerequisite for analyzing hyperspectral images (HSIs). While a multitude of conventional computational techniques employ GPUs to enhance efficiency and avoid closed-source limitations, these methods often obscure openness. Conversely, although deep learning-based approaches are frequently open and leverage GPUs, many researchers still find it challenging to apply them to real-world scenarios. Consequently, HyDe is presented as the industry's initial open-source software, written in GPU-accelerated Python, dedicated to denoising HSI. HyDe offers a diverse array of methods—spanning from low-rank wavelet-based strategies to deep neural networks—within an easily accessible framework that enhances both interoperability and execution speed. These optimized methods retain performance equivalent to their unoptimized originals but reduce energy consumption by approximately tenfold. Additionally, the project demonstrates that DNNs designed to denoise data collected from ground-level perspectives (such as aerial, drone, and satellite) can generalize effectively without needing training on those same perspectives. The application of trained DNNs is facilitated by a sliding window approach capable of efficiently processing large-scale HSI files that exceed 40 GB. The toolkit is available at: `\url{https://github.com/Helmholtz-AI-Energy/HyDe}`.

Biclustering represents a sophisticated data mining method capable of clustering both rows and columns within a matrix simultaneously. This approach facilitates visual analysis through a distinctive checkerboard pattern and is widely applicable. While various biclustering algorithms have emerged over the last twenty years—convex biclustering included, which guarantees an optimal result via convex optimization—practical applications have historically trailed behind these algorithmic advances. A notable lag exists in domains like microbiome research, which faces specific compositional constraints, leading to limited adoption of biclustering in this area. This manuscript introduces bi-ADMM, a new algorithm built on general ADMM principles and AD-MM frameworks that visualizes informative clusters free from the required extra-smoothing typical of existing methods tailored to convex constraints. Additionally, the algorithm is adapted as biC-ADMM, which directly addresses the compositional challenges intrinsic to dataset samples. A principal distinction between the proposed methods is the unique integration of the Sylvester equation within the ADMM derivation—a novelty in clustering literature—thereby eliminating the computational overhead of the AD-MM algorithm. The validity of the approach has been validated across numerous simulation studies and through a concrete case study of microbiome data application.

Organ motion remains an unresolved hurdle in image-guided interventions. To address this, the field of time-resolved volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (4D MRI) has developed; yet existing techniques fall short in typical interventional environments due to insufficient temporal or spatial resolution or prolonged acquisition times. We introduce a novel strategy for achieving real-time, high-resolution 4D imaging over a wide field of view for MR-guided interventions. By training an end-to-end convolutional neural network (CNN), we predict a 3D liver MRI representing the subject's respiratory phase based on live 2D navigator slices. This method offers two primary applications: first, reconstructing near real-time 4D images with high fidelity (209x128x128 matrix, 1.8 mm isotropic voxels) and at a resolution of approximately 6 seconds per volume for use during dynamic interventions guided by 2D navigation; second, enabling retrospective reconstruction for clinical scenarios like radiotherapy, with temporal resolutions better than 66.6 milliseconds, facilitating accurate motion analysis. Stack Stack Overflow serves not only as a repository for resolving programming issues but also as a platform enhancing developer competencies; thus, refining the caliber of inquiry posts has become a focal point. A succinct and accurate title is instrumental in conveying core information, directly elevating post quality, yet such titles often falter due to insufficient domain knowledge or weak compositional skills on the part of users. To remedy this gap, we introduce **SOTitle**, a framework designed to automatically generate post titles that synthesize information from both code snippets and problem narratives (multifodal data). To facilitate further exploration, we release the corpus and the system's code publicly for subsequent investigation.

Accelerated materials development tailored to specific properties represents a fundamental challenge in data-informed science. Traditional methods rely on data-driven paradigms that embed domain expertise via engineered feature descriptors, utilizing machine learning to map inputs to outputs. This paper introduces a synergistic computation framework merging mechanistic models with phenomenological and machine learning approaches to swiftly forecast the temperature-dependent yield strength of single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) high entropy alloys (HEAs).
