Enhancing how this framework addresses elastic mismatches is shown to be critical for the solid solution strengthening model, which underpins accurate strength predictions in the aforementioned alloys. By uniting ensemble machine learning with Bayesian inference, the study derives the probability distribution of these constants. Propagating this distribution yields both predicted yield strength curves and associated uncertainties, demonstrating strong alignment with existing experimental records. These results validate the proposed methodology for efficiently discovering new low-alloy alloys that exhibit superior strength across a wide temperature range.

Gradient leakage attacks constitute among the most severe privacy risks in deep learning, allowing malicious actors to covertly eavesdrop on gradient updates throughout training without degrading model accuracy; nonetheless, they can successfully infer sensitive data with significant efficacy. Although differential privacy remains the industry standard for secure model publication, this paper demonstrates that DP algorithms utilizing static privacy configurations are susceptible to gradient leakage, thereby undermining their protection. We examine novel strategies to achieve resilient performance, first by evaluating existing DP implementations that employ fixed noise variance for gradient injection via static privacy parameters. These methods offer DP confidentiality but often yield reduced model accuracy while failing to prevent gradient leakage exposure driven by consistent noise. We then introduce an adaptive DP framework featuring gradient leakage mitigation, which replaces rigid parameterization with dynamic privacy controls. This dynamic approach generates variable noise quantities adjusted to align with the evolving trajectory of gradients during the model training process. Finally, the study outlines four supplementary metrics designed to assess and contrast various privacy-preserving approaches regarding resilience against leakage while minimizing performance overhead.

Data harvested from industrial equipment frequently presents imbalance, a factor that undermines the efficacy of learning algorithms. This challenge is intensified further when data involves mixed types or exhibits inter-class overlapping. Addressing this disparity necessitates an adaptive learning system capable of prompt and reliable data prediction and classification. This study introduces a novel adversarial network tailored for joint classification and fault detection. Specifically, the model re-establishes dataset balance by synthesizing fault cases derived from a targeted mixture of data distributions. To mitigate outliers and curtail overfitting when processing these artificial faults, the model's discriminator was specifically architected to manage generated samples. Empirical findings substantiate that (i) the generator-driven discriminator can function effectively as a self-contained anomaly detector by distinguishing between normal and synthesized fault distributions; and (ii) the synthesized fault quality surpasses that of existing synthetic oversampling strategies. Comparative evaluations indicate that the proposed approach excels relative to various fault diagnosis techniques based on multiple metrics, with particular efficacy stemming from the synergy between the generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture and a novel feature matching mechanism in identifying anomalous samples.

Identifying user intent and extracting associated slots are central challenges within Natural Language Understanding (NLU). Traditionally, addressing zero-shot learning involves leveraging representations from pretrained multilingual transformers like mBERT, or machine-translating source texts into a known target language for fine-tuning. Our study targets scenarios where the target language is unidentified during training. We propose a novel strategy to augment monolithic training data with multilingual random translations of various language codes, thereby increasing a transformer model's linguistic neutrality during fine-tuning for downstream applications. Additionally, this approach yields new understandings on how code-switching across diverse linguistic families influences accuracy in the target language. Testing on the MultiATIS++ benchmark dataset demonstrates our method's superior performance when benchmarked against existing solutions and SOTAs across 8 languages, achieving a 4.2% average accuracy gain for intent prediction and a 1.8% improvement in F1 scores for entity extraction. Moreover, we apply this technique to the domain of crisis management, utilizing a freshly annotated Twitter dataset detailing English and Haitian Creole slot-filling from responses to the Haiti earthquake disaster.

The encoding phase scans the full temporal duration specifically for extreme events relative to a selected quantile-threshold, converting the original return series into Bernoulli-variable processes. Subsequently, the decoding phase employs an advanced newly designed search strategy coupled with information criteria applied to the resulting recurrence times to determine the locations of changes; this allows for dependency analysis while only relying on standard requirements for a Geometric distribution. Notably, this approach can divide a return series into homogeneous segments without enforcing assumptions regarding dynamic structures or specific data distributions. Empirical tests demonstrate favorable results against parametric alternatives like the Hidden Markov Model, while real-world applications aim to uncover short-range stock orderings before forecasting. Furthermore, the method reveals individual stock volatility dynamics for every S&P500 component and constructs a stock-network graph representing dependency relations based on simultaneous volatility states across the index.

Over the past ten years, accuracy on the ImageNet dataset has served as a key metric for tracking advancements in computer vision. Although recent research has increasingly debated the benchmark's practical utility, ongoing innovations continue to drive performance gains, pushing the largest contemporary models above 90% top-1 accuracy. To better interpret such milestones and establish meaningful evaluation criteria, we systematically examined and categorized the errors made only by top-performing models, shedding light on the long-tail distribution within this premier benchmark. Focusing particularly on the multi-label subset—where leading models now reach over 97% accuracy—our analysis reveals that nearly half of initially identified errors are valid under closer inspection, highlighting many newly discovered correct multi-labels. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that without rigorous validation, these top-performing systems have likely been significantly underestimated. Nevertheless, a substantial portion of their predictions (approximately 40%) remain glaringly incorrect from a human expert's perspective. To recalibrate our outlook for future progress, we present a refined multi-label evaluation dataset alongside ImageNet-Major. ImageNet-Major consist of 68 curated examples representing clear model failures, a subset where near-flawless performance is achievable yet remains elusive.

Catastrophic forgetting (CF) arises when training a neural network on data from a different distribution causes the loss of previously acquired knowledge; a phenomenon commonly encountered in task incremental settings. Although existing methods have shown promise in alleviating CF within these incremental scenarios—which are often not reflective of real-world applications—research addressing more practical, realistic contexts remains limited. To bridge this gap, we introduce Centroids Matching, an efficient regularization technique inspired by meta-learning principles that combats CF by manipulating feature space outputs directly. By comparing samples' feature vectors with class-specific centroids from current or cumulative tasks, this approach quickly mitigates forgetting with minimal memory requirements, especially when classification leverages the neural network’s internal feature outputs directly. It outperforms comparable baselines in speed and efficacy, maintaining distances in both previous embedding spaces preserved and present ones generated. Notably, while no external memory is needed for straightforward instances, modest memory reserves support its robustness in complex, realistic settings. Comprehensive experimental results validate our method's superior accuracy performance across diverse datasets.

Hybrid multiscale modelling represents an emerging and powerful framework for investigating intricate biological processes; however, incorporating stochastic internal agent dynamics often renders these simulations computationally demanding. While traditional methods can diminish the computational load for such models, they frequently compromise the fidelity and richness of the observed dynamics relative to the original system. To address this, we apply large deviation theory to lower the computational cost of spatially extended multi-agent stochastic systems by mapping them to a continuous time Markov chain defined over the original system's stable steady states. This coarse-grained approach maintains a precise representation of stable states while capturing noise-induced transitions between them. Using cell specification driven by lateral inhibition in a bistable framework as a test case, we demonstrate that the method facilitates the exploration of various pattern configurations and reveals robust emergent patterns at extended time scales. Furthermore, we benchmark the proposed coarse-grained strategy against full stochastic and mean-field descriptions using pattern quantification criteria and computational cost assessments to evaluate performance. Results indicate that the coarse-grained system offers the most efficient computational cost while successfully retaining the rich dynamics characteristic of stochastic models. Ultimately, this technique has the prospect of significantly alleviating complexities associated with large hybrid multiscale modellers, enhancing their suitability for rigorous numerical experimentation and hypothesis testing.

LiDAR point clouds deliver abundant geometric details, making them valuable for analyzing the complex structures found in urban environments. Detecting changes in both topology and semantics across two distinct three-dimensional scans of the same area, obtained at separate time points, constitutes a critical challenge. Traditionally, such comparative analysis relies on computationally intensive registration and segmentation steps. However, we aim to identify variations in geometric uncertainty and semantic information by avoiding the registration stage entirely. Consequently, we introduce an orientation-invariant geometric signature for the point cloud that synthesizes probabilistic semantic and geometric classification data. We investigate various characteristics of this signature, utilizing it as an image-based representation of the underlying uncertainty and semantic load. By examining multiple metrics designed to measure discrepancies between these signatures to establish differences among point clouds without point-to-point registration, we demonstrate in our findings that signature disparities align closely with actual differences in both geometry and semantics.

This work investigates the topic of robustness against adversarial attacks within the domain of offline reinforcement learning (RL). Starting with an inductive batch of tuple data $(s, a, r, s')$, an adversary has the capability to tamper with an arbitrary $\epsilon$ portion of these entries. Using this compromised dataset, the learner's objective is to robustly derive a near-optimal policy. Initially, the authors demonstrate that even with linear Markov Decision Processes (linear MDP) of dimensionality $d$, the adversary forces an irreparable optimality gap of at worst-order $\Omega(d\epsilon)$ in instances containing linear corruption affecting only the reward values within the information tuples. This result diverges from the corruption-robustness outcomes found in supervised learning, which remain constant relative to the input dimension and online reinforcement learning, which allows for the best-known lower bounds. Subsequently, the authors put forward robust modifications to the Least-Square Value Iteration (LSVI) method by deploying supervised learning models of robustness as oracles, which delivers performance levels comparable to the original approach whether using datasets with complete support coverage or those without. However, designing a pessimism bonus in unsupervised cases necessulates awareness of the corruption level $\epsilon$. Interestingly, the authors demonstrate that as such $\epsilon$ is unknown, adaptation is impossible even with no full support coverage. Contrary to the recent advances in resilience to adversarial perturbations in online reinforcement learning, the authors argue that robustness against attacks offline in RL is a problem distinctively more stringent.

Although contemporary image captioning systems achieve high coherence and precision, and ongoing advances in continual learning mitigate catastrophic forgetting in deep neural networks, the intersection of these domains remains underexplored. This study introduces a new domain defined as continuous image captioning and presents ContCap—a framework designed to generate captions across sequential tasks while seamlessly integrating continual learning to prevent forgetting. After establishing that catastrophic forgetting affects image captioning, we develop multiple mitigation techniques beyond a standard simple fine-tuning approach. Experiments utilizing the MS-COCO 2014 benchmark in class-incremental settings, which require no access to historical datasets, demonstrate significant improvements in performance on previously learned tasks, and surprisingly exceed the results of fine-tuning alone when evaluated on new tasks. Additionally, the proposed system offers a scalable architecture applicable to captioning both images and videos in continuous learning environments.

This study examines a multi-user multiple-input single-output (MISO) communications system aided by a hybrid active-passive reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). To ensure a fairness-centric design, we maximize the minimum data rate achievable by all users through joint optimization of transmit beamforming vectors and RTS phase shifts/amplifying weights. Employing stochastic convex approximation coupled with block coordinate ascent, we efficiently address the inherent nonconvexity, yielding computational efficiency through a complex, low-computational stepwise solution. Numerical findings reveal that a hybrid RIS comprising 4 actives out of a full set of 50, operating under a power limit of -1 dBm, achieves performance gains reaching as high as 80%; in contrast, a purely passive RIS delivers merely a 27% boost under the given conditions.

This paper resolves this by introducing a single-loop Accelerated Constrained Gradient Descent (ACGD) method. ACGD adapts AGD by replacing the standard descent with a constrained one, requiring an augmented set of simple linear constraints within the proximity operator analysis. This algorithm attains nearly identical oracle complexity as the theoretical minimum for optimizing the Lagrangian with a fixed optimal multiplier $\lambda^*$. We demonstrate these upper-bound complexities are tight, supported by new matching lower bounds under specific regime conditions. For scaling to large problems with numerous function constraints, an iterative variant known as Sliding Accelerated Constrained Gradient Descent (ACGD-S) replaces expensive constrained projections with efficient sequences of matrix-vector multiplications. Remarkably, ACGD-S preserves the same oracle complexity as the standard version while achieving theoretically unimproved complexity for the required number of matrix operations.

The research area of learning-to-rank is highly valued by the academic machine learning community owing to its critical applications in information retrieval, data mining, and natural language processing, making both accurate ranking and the learning-to-rank paradigm essential. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have revolutionized machine learning, while differential privacy (DP) has established itself as a standard method for safeguarding data secrecy. Merging these technologies enables the deployment of high-performance models trained on sensitive information, such as medical data; this is typically achieved using DP-SGD, a private variant of the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimizer. Although later studies have optimized noise decay architectures, features, or hyperparameters, the foundational mechanism within DP-SGD that enforces privacy remains original, acting as a persistent constraint on the efficacy of privacy-preserving machine learning. Addressing this limitation, we introduce DPIS, a new differentially private SGD training mechanism designed to replace the DP-SGD core optimizer as a plug-in while offering significant and consistent accuracy improvements. DPIS achieves these results by utilizing importance sampling (IS) for mini-batch selection within each iteration, thereby reducing sampling variance and the volume of noise necessary to satisfy privacy guarantees despite being challenging to integrate into existing DP complexity solutions. Successfully deploying DPIS required creating novel designs, conducting fine-grained privacy analyses, boosting computational efficiency, and introducing adaptive gradient clipping optimization. Extensive testing on four benchmark datasets—MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and IMDb—illustrates that DPIS markedly outperforms current approaches in the field of privacy-preserving deep learning.

Acquisition of new skills via human behavioral observation constitutes a pivotal ability for AI systems. In this study, we exploit instructional videos to investigate human decision-making, specifically aiming to develop models capable of planning goal-oriented actions within real-life footage. Unlike traditional action recognition, which identifies movements, goal-directed actions rely on anticipations of results and necessitate a causal grasp of how actions influence their environments. Consequently, effectively integrating environmental structure with specific objectives is vital for addressing this challenging task. Existing approaches, which rely on a single world model, often fail to differentiate between distinct scenarios, leading to an ambiguous latent representation; as planning progresses through this model, a loss of future goal-related global information tends to cause these desired outcomes to be undervalued. Overcoming these shortcomings, we propose an updated framework for procedure planning and introduce advanced algorithms utilizing Bayessian Inference alongside model-based imitation learning to replicate human conduct. Empirical evaluations utilizing real-world instructional demonstrations reveal that our approach achieves leading-edge performance in achieving stated objectives, with the derived contextual data exhibiting valuable structural properties for effective latent-space planning.

Notably, DEM offers a key benefit in reducing the computational burden of approximated higher-order derivatives associated with formulations based exclusively on strong form residuals. Nevertheless, both standard DeeP Learning Energy Methods and classical PINNs alike face limitations when resolving fine-grained concentration features within stress or displacement fields in solid mechanics applications. We present an extension of DEM tailored for finite strain hyperelasticity to overcome these resolution limits. Our proposed mixed Deep Energy Method (mDEM) enhances the recently developed pure displacement framework by incorporating stress measures as a supplementary neural network output. This augmentation improves the accuracy of Neumann boundary condition enforcement and significantly boosts performance around spatial regions responsible for material concentrations. Furthermore, to enhance versatility, we implemented a numerical integration routine utilizing Delaunay triangulation, thereby enabling the mDEM architecture to handle irregular training point distributions frequently encountered in domains with stress concentrations. We demonstrate through comparative analysis the superior merits of our approach alongside the persisting deficits of traditional PINN and DEM formulations. The mDEM delivers results comparable to standard Finite Element Method (FEM) during the forward prediction of difficult simulations involving complex geometric configurations and concentrated loads.

System-level transportation decision-making requires accounting for daily fluctuations in network flows, necessitating robust probabilistic modeling of dynamic travel demand. While most current approaches focus on deterministic dynamic origin-destination (OD) demand, often neglecting these variations, accurate probabilistic estimation remains a challenge due to the complexity and computational burden of spatio-temporal, high-dimensional problems. Leverage on vast datasets and advanced computational technologies, this study introduces a data-driven PDODE (Probabilistic Dynamic OD Demand Estimation) solution utilizing multi-day traffic data. Various statistical metrics, including lp-norm, KL divergence, Bhattacharyya distance, and Wasserstein distance, were employed and evaluated, revealing that 2-Wasserstein distance effectively balances mean estimation with variance (standard deviation). Implemented within a computational graph with a specialized reparameterization trick, the proposed method simultaneously calibrates the mean and standard deviation of dynamic OD demand. Validated on both microscopic and real-world large-scale networks, the framework demonstrates enhanced efficiency and reduced overfitting by incorporating demand uncertainty. In conclusion, this PDODE framework offers public agencies a powerful tool to decipher demand stochasticity sources and assess daily flow variability, enabling more reliable decision support for intelligent transportation systems.

Gaussian process regression has become an essential technique within model predictive control (MPC) forecasts for predicting disturbances and addressing mismatches by embedding this data directly into the prediction model. However, a major bottleneck is the cubic scaling of inference and learning operations for traditional Gaussian processes (GPs), causing them to become computationally prohibitive for real-time use; consequently, they are often restricted to offline pre-trading, where they fail to adapt dynamically when disturbances evolve over time. To overcome these limitations, state-space-formulating GPs were introduced as a solution that reduces both inference and learning to linear computational complexity. The studies here details a new framework tailored for executing online disturbance modeling of four-chains within a millisecond timeframe via state-space GP representation using quadcopter platforms in a simulated environment via JMAVSIM. Approaches utilizing geometric methods to learn occupancy and metric maps excel at generalization for solving open-world off-road navigation; however, they can become unstable in outdoor settings where underlying assumptions are breached, such as areas of tall grass. Conversely, learning-based techniques can directly extract collision-free behaviors from raw sensory data but pose significant integration challenges when combined with traditional geometric frameworks. This leads to a problematic compromise where engineers must choose between relying entirely on learning (sacrificing known geometric advantages) or adhering purely to geometry, which often demands laborious manual adjustment of cost functions rather than utilizing machine learning. Our work resolves this false dichotomy by architecting both learned and geometric components to function in unison within a self-supervised paradigm. Both parts feed into the planning process, where the learned element supplies traversability predictions as rewards and the geometric module provides explicit obstacle costs. Through instantiation and comparative analysis in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios, we demonstrate that this hybrid architecture leverages the complementary strengths of both components to deliver significantly superior performance compared to either approach used alone. Videos of our findings are available at https://sites.google.com/view/hybrid-imitative-planning.

We study the problem of last-mile delivery, involving a significant network of crowd-workers employed for various location-based urban parcel logistics. Existing methodologies concentrate on offline contexts in which the spatiotemporal details of both packages and workers are known beforehand. However, these offline approaches often prove impractical because, within real-world operations, parcels emerge only dynamically and lack predetermined information. This study aims to address the limitations of static settings by formally defining the online variant where packages are pre-stocked in pickup stations while workers arrive in a dynamic flow. Subsequently we design an algorithm capable of theoretically guaranteeing the quality of such dynamic allocations. Finally, through experiments on both real-world and simulated data sets, we evaluate the resulting algorithm's effectiveness and runtime efficiency.

Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation partitions an image based on textual descriptions, even when those categories were not encountered during training. While current two-stage pipelines create region proposals and use Vision-Language models like CLIP to label them, we found that CLIP is often the performance bottleneck because its standard inputs perform poorly on masked images our method generates. We introduce the strategy of refining CLIP on datasets constructed from masked image crop and their linked text descriptions. By "scraping" noun-text alignments for masked crops from established caption sets (such as COCO Captions), we build a training resource that, despite containing noise and exhibiting lower precision than supervised standards like COCO-Stuff, offers more variety and effectively maintains CLIP's generalization capacity. Beyond full model fine-tuning on the entire CLIP architecture, we also implement a technique called "mask prompt tuning" to exploit the unmasked areas of segmented images without altering any pre-trained weights. Experimental results show that this prompt tuning alone delivers substantial gains and yields even better outcomes in synergy with fine-tuning. Notably, training on COCO data and testing on ADE20k-150 allows a model with an mIoU reaching 29.6%—a +8.5% improvement over the prior state-of-the-art—to reach the performance of open-vocabulary generalists matching specialist models from 2017. Crucially, we achieve specialized-level performance in 1517 without needing model adaptations to the A20k domain specific dataset.

Consequently, the system undergoes localization on the spatial scale of $\sqrt{D/|\mu|}$, where $\mu$ represents the symmetry-breaking strength and $D$ serves as the effective diffusion parameter associated with the restored antisymmetric configuration.

We investigate reinforcement learning tasks encoded via reward machines. These tasks are defined over environmental atomic propositions, represented asBoolean variables, though a common literature assumption—that truth values are perfectly accurate—is often impractical for real-world scenarios involving imperfect sensors. Furthermore, reward machines for complex tasks can be intractably difficult to model manually. Accordingly, we introduce a reinforcement learning algorithm that simultaneously infers the reward machine encoding a task and learns execution methods despite proposition uncertainties. This algorithm manages uncertainty by maintaining probabilistic estimates of atomic proposition truth values that update based on continuous sensory measurements from environmental exploration. Concurrently, it sustains a hypothesis reward machine, estimating the target machine, and updates this hypothesis upon observing rewards correlated with updated proposition estimates. Finally, the system employs Q-learning across the states of this hypothesis reward to determine the task-accomplishing policy. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the proposed method successfully recovers the reward model and converges asymptotically to a policy capable of achieving the intended task.

The rise of Convolutional Neural Network-based (CNN) steganalysis methods presents a significant threat to steganography. Although embedding cost learning using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has proven successful in spatial domains and remains in its prototype stage for JPEG steganography, there is potential for enhanced anti-detectability and training efficiency. Traditionally, security can be bolstered using side-information derived from precovs, but this requires the spatial domain image which is typically unavailable. This study proposes an embedding cost learning framework called JS-Embed (or similar) for JPEG steganography leveraging GMAN (Generative Adversarial Networks). The learned embedding cost is dynamically adjusted based on estimated side-information, resulting in highly personalized, content-adaptable cost functions. Testing with the GFR steganoAnalyzer (Qf=75 and 2.0 bpnpx) revealed a significant security enhancement: not only is detection accuracy improved compared to the current best practice models using the estimated side-information, achieving higher performance metrics than standard methods in various experimental settings, but also, the addition of this technique further fortifies detection robust against advanced classifiers across multiple test configurations. The proposed method not only helps maintain security but also improves overall system efficiency and reliability.

This research introduces a generalized framework for convolution operations. Given a finite domain $D$, we define a set $D^n$ representing vectors of length $n$ from $D$. For a function $f : D \times D \to D$, we define a coordinate-wise operation $\oplus_f$. The $f$-Convolution between two functions mapping $D^n$ to a value range is a sum of products over pairs of vector arguments that produce the target output when combined via $\oplus_f$. While this concept encompasses fundamental problems like Covering/Product Packing/Subset/XOR convolutions, previous methods relied on brute-force enumeration requiring $\widetilde{O}(|D|^{2n}\mathrm{polylog}(M))$ time.

We present a significant algorithmic improvement, computing $f$-Convolution in $\widetilde{O}((c \cdot |D|^2)^{n}\mathrm{polylog}(M))$ time exactly when the domain cardinality is even and $c = 5/6$. The Pigeonhole Principle (PHP), both theoretically and practically within automated reasoning, has undergone significant study; most solvers exhibit exponential complexity regarding runtime and proof width, though specialized approaches manage to achieving polynomial complexities. A Davydov D2-based Dirac-Frenkel variational approach for simulating dynamic open quantum systems has been expanded with a novel thermalization protocol. This algorithm enables precise control over temperature fluctuations within a harmonic finite-sized bath coupled to the primary system. By utilizing stochastic scattering modeled as a discrete-time Bernoulli process following Poisson statistics, the method steers vibrational modes toward their canonical thermal equilibrium, thereby achieving temperature equilibration of bath modes. Analysis of exciton relaxation within a compact molecular cluster demonstrates not only the efficacy of this equilibration process but also a marked computational efficiency, attributable to the significantly reduced number of vibrational modes required for convergence.

Reversible spreading mechanisms involving re-infection are prevalent across natural systems and societal contexts, evident in phenomena such as gonorrhea dissemination and the propagation of memes. Pinpointing key diffusion drivers represents a crucial challenge within the dynamics of reversible processes on complex networks, a subject that has garnered considerable attention. Beyond standard structural centrality, a node's dynamic state is vital for assessing its ability to spread. To address this, a novel metric is formulated that fuses a node's outgoing edge count with aggregated neighbor infection risks into structural centrality; this metric encapsulates the interplay where structure and dynamical status jointly determine influence within the propagation cycle. In this framework, the volume of outgoing edges reflects the positive impact of local structural features on spreading potential, as do the neighbor risk metrics regarding opposing effects from node dynamics; specifically, these factors represent the positive influence of local network topology and the negative influence of inherent node instability, respectively. Our analysis reveals that optimally merging these two distinct characteristics significantly enhances the precision of the measure in detecting dominant spreaders. Foreword, a marginal reduction in the negative weight assigned to a node's dynamic states, relative to a strong emphasis on positive local structural features, optimizes the measure's efficacy. Ultimately, achieving quantitative insight into how structure and dynamism comparatively impact node influence offers meaningful direction for identifying key agents in reversible diffusion systems.

While mechanical metamaterials facilitate unique functions, passive versions are often constrained by their baseline energy levels, requiring separate energy supply for repeated operation. This study presents a theoretical framework for an active mechanical metamaterial utilizing a biological reaction mechanism to address this limitation in passive systems. Our material supports reversible signal transmission by recovering energy through the bio-inspired mechanism; by analyzing a continuum analogue of the discrete system as a coarse-grained model, we demonstrate that mechanical signals propagate via traveling waves. Investigating the continuous model identifies the specific parameter regions conducive to signal transmission and uncovers analogies to the FitzHugh-Nagumo system, which characterists neuron-like excitability. Furthermore, we provide explicit expressions approximating how the timescale of the biological reaction influences signal transmission speed, a critical factor in controlling the material's dynamics.

To address this, this study introduces a novel, adaptable liquidity mining mechanism. It achieves global liquidity distribution by precisely regulating local rewards alone. From the perspective of providers supplying liquidity, their allocation strategies shape a multiperson competitive equilibrium. By analyzing the Nash Optimal Point for this dynamic, especially in isolated instances by matching liquidity provision directly with reward allocation (which broadly addresses complex scenarios as well), this approach offers a way for miners to direct provider strategies, potentially lowering slippage on demand and maintaining greater price stability.

Accurately simulating phonons is crucial for understanding thermal characteristics in next-gen ultra-scaled CMOS and thermoelectric devices. This paper outlines a modified valence force field (MVFF) approach, detailing its implementation for calculating phonon dispersion across zinc-blende materials. The framework transitions seamlessly from infinite crystals (bulk) to nanostructures (nanowires) once suitable boundary conditions are included. However, computational complexity escalates sharply as the wire's cross-sectional dimensions grow. Generating plausible and controllable 3D human motion animations is a persistent challenge that has historically required skilled human artists. Although contemporary machine learning techniques offer semi-automation, they remain significantly constrained: typically supporting only a single expected motion trajectory, which restricts fine-grained control over the results. To address this limitation, the problem of future pose prediction is reframed as pose filling in both temporal and spatial dimensions; in this view, multiple potential trajectories are modeled as poses containing unidentified joints. This approach yields a generalization framework applicable across different architechures originally designed for future pose prediction. Once trained within this structure, a resulting system is able to predict motion sequences derived from an unlimited number of distinct trajectories. We introduce TrajeVAE, a new architecture inspired by transformers that leverages this concept to establish a flexible platform for 3D animation. Empirical results indicate that TrajeVAE achieves superior performance compared both to reference trajectory methods and those relying on past poses alone for predictions. Furthermore, findings suggest it is capable of generating credible future pose sequences based solely on an input initial position.

The core principle underlying strongly correlated quantum matter—spanning fractional quantum Hall liquids, optical-lattice atoms, and twisted bilayer graphene—is the supremacy of interactions over kinetic energy. Crystalline phases frequently rival these correlated quantum fluids; the boundary between them forms when the energy required to generate a density wave vanishes. A quintessential instance involves electrons under strong magnetic fields, where the fragility of quantum Hall liquids leading toward a Wigner crystal is signaled by a roton-like softening of density waves matching the magnetic length size. Notably, theoretical predictions also propose that interacting bosons coupled to a synthetic gauge field can develop analogous liquid and solid phases. Yet, achieving experimental access involving combined interactions and strong synthetic magnetism with bosonic quantum gases remains difficult.

In response to these constraints, our work examines purely interaction-driven behavior within a Landau-gauged Bose-Einstein condensate located near and within the lowest Landau level (LLL). We document a spontaneous transition into a crystal state triggered by the condensation of magneto-rotons—a class of excitations identifiable by magnetic-scale density undulations. Furthermore, raising the cloud's density gradually bridges this behavior to a quantum analogue of the Kelvin-Helmholtz hydrodynamic instability. This later stage arises from sheared flows inherent in the rapid internal rotation of the condensate. Over extended durations, the system self-assembles into a long-lasting array of isolated droplets, interspersed between vortex streets. This configuration remains stable due to a delicate equilibrium between interaction forces and those generated by an effective magnetic repulsion.

Quantum systems with spherical symmetry, including the hydrogen atom, appear to lack an exact analytical solution in high-dimensional frames. However, compactifying certain dimensions potentially allows this issue to be resolved. This work investigates spherical symmetry quantum models within non-commutative spacetime featuring extra compact dimensions. Specifically, we analytically derive the spectrum for hydrogen and Yukawa problems using a 4+1 non-commutative spacetime under the first order approximation of non-commutativity, and further consider cases where $D \geq 4$.

Diffusive dynamics involving profound energy wells and weak nongradient forces streamline into a mesoscopic jump process transitioning across distinct basinos of attraction. By uniting classical weak-noise theory with path integral expansions centered at equilibrium, we demonstrate that the resulting transition probabilities adhere strictly to the local detailed balance (LDB) principle. Specifically, the logarithmic ratio of jump rates between neighboring attractor basins mirrors the equilibrium free-energy difference, augmented by the work exerted by nonconservative forces along typical transition trajectories. Furthermore, if the mesoscopic dynamics exhibit a large-scale deterministic limit, they can descend even further to a macroscopic jump protocol. Ultimately, the resilience of local detailed balance during coarse graining within near-equilibrium systems stems generically from the fact that dissipative mechanisms alone dictate behavior near equilibrium.

Utilizing smart network hardware within datacenters is an emerging trend. Current high-performance switches are being engineered to support near-line-rate computation and aggregation, catering to advanced applications such as big data analytics and expansive distributed or federated machine learning initiatives. We address the challenge of optimally activating a restricted quantity of these in-network processing units to minimize network congestion for a specific workload. Constraints on deploying multiple processing elements often stem from scenarios like phased infrastructure upgrades, necessitating for specialized firmware appliances (FPGAs) capable of accommodating various heterogeneous tasks and multi-tenancy situations. We detail an optimal, high-efficiency algorithm for device placement specifically adapted to tree networks with non-uniform link rates. Experimental assessments across multiple scenarios and tasks reveal that empowering only a small minority of network nodes with aggregation capabilities can drastically lower overall network utilization. Additionally, we demonstrate that straightforward heuristics for device placement consistently yield poorer results than our proposed method across differing workloads, processing demands, and link configurations.

This study rigorously examines the excitation spectra of an attractive spin-1/2 Fermi gas (the Yang-Gaudin model) using the exact Bethe ansatz solution. Elementary excitations in this context comprise particle-hole excitations, hole excitations, as well as particles added to the Fermi seas of both paired and unpaired fermions. While gapped magnons within the spin sector exhibit ferromagnetic coupling to the Fermi sea of single fermions, we employ numerical and analytical methods to solve the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz equations for the model across various polarizations in a Felule-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) phase. In the strong coupling and long-wavelength regime, analytical solutions yield the linear dispersion, curvature terms, velocities, and effective masses for particle-hole excitations in both paired and unpaired sectors. These collective modes reveal a novel separation between the bosonic movements of fermion pairs and unpaired particles. Additionally, we address spin-sector magnon excitations and propose the application of Bragg spectroscopy to verify distinct charge excitation modes associated with singles and pairs fermion systems.

Consequently, our theoretical work lays a foundation for future practical advancements without compromising the reliability of correctness guarantees.

Event cameras, owing to their high temporal resolution and extensive dynamic range, offer unique advantages for analyzing time-periodic visual signals. In this study, we introduce a fully asynchronous algorithm designed for these cameras to identify the fundamental flicker frequency of pixels within an image stream. Additionally, we show that analyzing signal falling edges yields higher estimation precision than using rising edges, while zero-level crossing interpolation can further enhance accuracy for specific inputs. Our experimental results highlight a significant disparity: although the camera can reliably detect frequencies up to 64 kHz per single pixel in controlled tests, full-frame sensor imaging is severely hindered by readout bandwidth limitations. These findings imply that shifting the processing closer to the sensor hardware would substantially boost frequency imaging capabilities, which is discussed alongside optimal design parameters for this purpose. We also present "Frequency Cam" (https://github.com/berndpfrommer/frequency_cam), an open-source ROS-compatible implementation capable of processing over 50 million events per second on a single laptop core using CPU-only computation. Traditional wireless systems typically fail to facilitate multimedia communication meeting specific Quality of Service standards unless they secure a contiguous frequency band wide enough for the needed bandwidth. To address this constraint in Cognitive Radio Networks, we propose a novel channel allocation strategy. This approach employs multiple disjoint channels, where each individually lacks sufficient width but, in aggregate, meet or exceed the total bandwidth demand. Our work details algorithms for sensation, reservation, and release of channels, alongside transmission and reception protocols utilizing $FDM-FDMA$ and $OFDM-FDMA$. Simulation outcomes for these implementations indicate that the suggested technique surpasses existing first-fit and best-fit allocation methods~\cite{b109, b110}. This outperformance is observed across all traffic conditions ranging from low to extreme, specifically regarding the reduced attempts required to gather the adequate number of channels. Notably, the new technique successfully allocates the needed channels within one second using $FDM-FDMA$ and within $4.5$ seconds using $OFDM-FDMA$, handling traffic loads up to 96%, whereas conventional first-fit and best-fit approaches are unable to allocate any resources under the same high-load conditions.

This study tackles the challenge of equipping deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents to execute instructions across multi-task settings. Commands are formulated using linear temporal logic (LTL), a formal language capable of encoding varied, temporally extended behaviors with complex structures like conditionals and multiple alternative interpretations. The proposed algorithm harnesses the compositional semantics and syntax of LTL, allowing the RL agent to develop task-specific policies that successfully generalize to unseen instructions not present during training. To alleviate the costs associated with learning LTL principles, we implement an environment-agnostic pre-training strategy for LTL, thereby enhancing sample efficiency within subsequent downstream tasks. Experiments spanning both discrete and continuous domain target a combinatorial set of up to ~10^39 distinct tasks, illustrating our method's efficacy in solving (previously unseen) tasks based on provided LTL directives.

Protein stability is fundamental to protein fitness, and its alteration via targeted mutation holds significant implications across protein engineering, drug design, and the annotation of damaging variants. Over the past several decades, numerous research efforts have focused on developing novel AI-driven techniques to enhance the prediction of how mutations affect stability. In this discussion, we examine the characteristics, algorithms, computational performance, and predictive precision—assessed on independent test datasets—of current approaches, while critiquing persistent biases toward training data, generalizability issues, interpretability, and a stagnation in accuracy near the 1 kcal/mol level over the past fifteen years. Finally, our conclusions address the obstacles required for achieving superior prediction performance.

Similarly, for high $u_0$, we determine $t_{\rm max}\propto u_0^\beta$ with $\beta \approx -0.5$. While these power-law behaviors remain consistent across various system sizes for $u_0 > \text{large values}$, the rebound event is sensitive to container depth in suspension. Consequently, we argue that the rebound is not directly coupled to the scaling relations involving $u_0$, $F_{\rm max}$, and $t_{\rm max}$. We suggest a "floating + force chain" model, whereby the rebound is driven by an elastic component proportional to the count of connected force paths from impactor to the bottom. The experimental observation of spin-pumped spin from a ferromagnetic insulator into a high-transition-temperature super conductor possessing a $d$-wave order parameter has established that unconventional superconductivity can generate interfacial bound states at specific crystallographic alignments. This work introduces a comprehensive approach for investigating spin transport into unconventional superconductors and the specific influence of such bound states. Using this framework, we analyzed how the angle of the interfacial $d$-wave order parameter modulates the spin-pumping effect. We identified that while orientations favoring interfacial bound states exhibit a marginal enhancement of spin pumping at low temperatures relative to other states, two key deviations appear: the absence of a standard coherence-peak enhancement near $T_c$, alongside a total effect remaining below normal state levels across all temperatures. Conversely, for non-favored orientations where bound states do not exist, the pumped spin current can surge to several multiples of the normal state current at low frequencies (relative to the energy gap). Ultimately, our findings indicate that both frequency and temperature dependencies of spin pumping undergo a qualitative transformation depending on the specific angular orientation of the unconventional superconducting gap.

Diagnosing cardiac arrhythmia requires the analysis and interpretation of electrocardiography (ECG) signals, for which machine learning has recently emerged as an effective tool for computer-aided automated diagnosis. These learning tasks generally categorize into two main types: regression and classification. Regression techniques assist in removing noise and artifacts, as well as addressing data gaps caused by low sampling frequencies. Conversely, classification tasks involve forecasting diagnostic output classes based on input labels established by medical experts. This study introduces a deep neural network capable of performing both regression and classification simultaneously. We integrated these two methodologies by leveraging a combination of labeled and unlabeled data for model training. Evaluated using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia database with modified Lead II ECG records, our approach demonstrated robust performance in both ECG signal approximation and arrhythmia detection. Regarding signal approximation (regression), the method achieved accurate QRS complex prediction. Leveraging self-supervised learning allowed this regression component to be trained without requiring expert annotations, facilitating a knowledge transfer strategy that improved the classification task. Ultimately, by transferring information from the regression process, our method achieved a total accuracy of 87:33% and balancing accuracy of at 20:32% when classifying cardiac conditions, which were results nearly equalled to existing reference methods, and further boosted to an overall classification accuracy of 29:32%.

As a component of a broader project designed to refine our knowledge of Galactic globular clusters near the central bulge and disk of the Milky Way, this research investigates the internal kinematics of nine such clusters based on over 9 years of spacecraft observations. We utilize several methods to evaluate their dynamics by creating radial profiles for projected stellar density, proper motion spread, and anisotropy. We suggest that two-thirds (or 6 of 9) of these clusters are approaching or have recently finished the process of core collapse. This conclusion draws on dual lines of evidence: the discovery of sharply rising proper motion dispersion profiles consistent with known core-collapsed systems, and the observation that most remain isotropic out to the half-light radius. Notable exceptions occur only for one system, NGC 6380, which shows slight tangential anisotropy beyond its core—a result aligning with theory regarding clusters subjected to intense tidal forces. Additionally, the profiles for both motion spread and anisotropy have been made public.

We propose a novel approach for pairwise alignment of neural fields by advancing classical local optimization registration methods (specifically, ICP), adapting them to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Since standard NeRF models fail to disentangle illumination from color—rendering them sensitive to lighting changes—we develop a "surface field," derived by distilling information from pre-trained NeRF models to estimate a point's surface probability. This method transforms NeRF-to-NeRF registration into a robust optimization problem, iteratively solving for a rigid transformation that aligns the respective surface fields of two scenes. Assessment involves testing against both classical techniques: synthetic data provides quantitative evaluation, while captured real-world instances confirm applicability in actual settings. More results and resources are available at {https://nerf2nerf.github.io}.

Electroencephalographic (EEG) signals offer rich insights into cerebral activities yet present challenges for analysis due to their heterogeneity and high dimensionality. Employing a priori knowledge can address dimensionality issues but risks discarding valuable patterns and information, leaving data heterogeneity as a persistent barrier to generalization. This study introduces a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for feature selection applicable to both supervised and unsupervised frameworks, evaluating performance through three distinct fitness functions derived without expert input. Utilizing public datasets on cognitive workload and motor control/imagery, we processed and normalized signals, calculating features across temporal, spectral, and time-frequency domains before applying our selection mechanism alongside benchmark methods. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance compared to benchmarks, particularly in overall efficacy and feature compression rates. Furthermore, when distinct datasets are merged, a novel fitness-specific GA instance exceeds benchmark results, validating the method's capability to handle diverse data effectively.

To overcome this barrier, our approach leverages compressed sensing: a method capable of reconstructing quantum states using only an incomplete set of observables. This paper presents an experimental demonstration of compressed tomography for a seven-qubit system, the largest scale achieved to date, aided by the development of new numerical protocols that allow reconstruction in such high-dimensional spaces.

Recent studies propose using deep learning for downlink power allocation in massive MIMO (maMIMO) systems, yet such models remain susceptible to adversarial threats. Over the past few years, parameterized quantum circuits have emerged as a primary method for constructing quantum algorithms aimed at solving optimization tasks. The significant challenge in deploying these circuits effectively stems from the difficulty of identifying suitable parameters within a non-convex energy landscape, whose volume expands exponentially as the count of variables increases.

To address this, we present a novel optimization framework for these circuits, which centers on rounding solutions derived from Semidefinite Programming (SDP). Using this approach, we detail an algorithm capable of generating approximate solutions for the "Quantum Max Cut" problem, a key type of quantum optimization task. Our proposed rounding method executes in polynomial time relative to the number of variables and remains efficient irrespective of the structure of the interaction graph applied. Consequently, this yields a 0.562-approximation algorithm for generic Quantum Max Cut instances, representing an advancement over prior methods that achieved only ratios below 0.54.

This paper proposes a novel framework for disentangling trends (drift) from change points (shifts) in time series analysis. The proposed methodology synergizes the benefits of both: combining the broad versatility of Bayesian DLMs with the rigorous "hard thresholding" capabilities of penalized estimators. A shortage of medical expertise to annotate imaging data has made developing label-efficient techniques for image segmentation a highly active area of research. In response, a novel framework is introduced: the labeled-efficient hybrid supervision model, which weights individual weakly annotated instances based on gradients derived from strongly annotated samples. By leveraging high-quality priors and improving descriptions of weaker instances using these directional gradients, the approach prevents such degradation. The Dynamic Instance Indicator (DII) encapsulates these mechanisms. When adapted within a Dynamic Co-Regularization (DCR) framework, it also mitigates error accumulation caused by weak annotation distorsions. Evaluations on two hybrid-supervised medical segmentation datasets show that with merely 10\% strong labels, this proposed framework utilizes weak labels efficiently, achieving competitive performance comparable to supervised models utilizing 100\% strong labels.

Due to their crystal inversion symmetry, it was generally presumed that Dirac semimetals could not exhibit the circular photogalvanic effect (CPGE). Contrarily, we document the emergence of the CPGE in $\text{Cd}_3\text{As}_2$ nanobelt field-effect transistors when illumination is targeted near metal contacts up to room temperature. Comprehensive experiments, including angularly and spatially resolved photocurrent helicity dependence, Kelvin probe force microscopy, and electrical gating, validate this hypothesis. Furthermore, first-principles simulations confirm that the local field induces structural distortions leading to a topological phase transition. These findings offer essential perspectives on electrically controlling helicity-dependent optoelectronic functionalities within Dirac materials.

Real-world language models (LMs) often enable human-AI collaboration, such as in programming autocomplete and drafting help; yet standard evaluation benchmarks remain static by generating output devoid of user input. Addressing the need for interactive assessment, we introduce HALIE (Human-AI Language-based Interaction Evaluation), a framework that extends non-interactive testing across three distinct dimensions: evaluating the interaction process as much as the final result, accounting for first-person user experience rather than sole reliance on external judgments, and incorporating preference criteria beyond just task quality. Our analysis employs five tasks varying from goal-specific to open-ended scenarios to explore diverse interaction forms. Tested on four leading models (including GPT-3 variants and J1-Jumbo), our results reveal that high scores in non-interactive tasks do not always translate to better collaborative performance, and that subjective user ratings can differ from objective third-party assessments. These findings underscore the critical importance of investigating the subtle details of how humans interact with LMs.

Assessing speech intelligibility is crucial for treating patients with pathological speech disorders. There is a growing desire for automatic, objective metrics to aid clinicians, whose current evaluations often rely on subjective and laborious analysis. This study introduces a new method for deriving such a measure by examining divergence within disentangled latent speech vectors derived from parallel utterances between healthy benchmarks and patients. Experiments conducted on an English database of individuals with Cerebral Palsy, utilizing complete datasets for each speaker, revealed a strong, significant correlation (R = -0.9) between our automated measure and subjective intelligibility ratings. Additionally, the method exhibited minimal deviation (±0.01) across four distinct reference pairs. We further confirmed the robustness of this approach by testing with a significantly smaller number of utterances, recording consistent correlation (R = -0.89 with deviations ±0.02 over 1000 iterations). Ultimately, these findings represent one of the first instances where disentangled speech representations have successfully been leveraged for automatic intelligibility assessment of pathological speech, yielding an invariant method against the choice of reference speakers that remains effective even with limited voice data.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operating within the Message Passing (MP) framework typically exchange information only among first-hop neighbors to construct node embeddings per layer. Fundamentally, these architectures cannot capture long-range interactions (LRI), which are often essential or beneficial for certain graph-learning tasks. Recently, research methods adapted from Transformer models for graphs have garnered significant attention specifically because they consider full node connectivity beyond the original sparse adjacency matrix, thereby facilitating LRI modeling. Nonetheless, MP-GNNs augmented merely through 1-hop message processing often outperform other approaches on current benchmarks when equipped with features such as positional encodings; this advantage restricts the relative standing and perceived viability of Transformer-like designs. To address this limitation, we introduce the Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB), comprised of five datasets—PascalVOC-SP, COCO-SP, PCQM-Contact (PC), Peptides-functions, and Peptides-structures—that likely require explicit long-range dependency modeling to achieve optimal results. Experimental evaluations compare baseline MP-GNNs and Graph Transformer models; the results demonstrate that models designed to capture long-range dependencies excel significantly on these tasks. Consequently, these datasets serve as a robust resource for the evaluation and prospective investigation of architectures for MP-GNNs and Graph Transformers aimed at addressing LRI.

Consequently, to observe weakly attenuated, quasi-flat plasmon excitations in these materials, one must achieve both an isolated flat band structure via lattice effects and the correct hole-doping level. Future investigations into superconductivity in these systems may thus be fruitfully examined in light of these plasmonic findings.

Stars and planets both undergo mass loss via extended wind flows, often regulated by the surrounding magnetosphere created by trapping or channel magnetic fields. While the powerful winds of massive stars result primarily from radiative momentum transferred through spectral lines, the feebleer mass loss in solar and less massive stars stems from thermal expansion triggered by the mechanical heating of a corona. For planets orbiting these low-mass stars, the interaction of stellar radiative heating with winds can induce atmospheric heating or even ablation. The formation mechanisms diverge between stellar environments, where magnetosphemes form from trapping outgoing winds internally, whereas planetary magnetosphemes are primarily deformed by the external force of stellar winds. Despite these differences, the stresses exerted on both systems frequently trigger magnetic reconnection events, producing diagnostics such as X-ray flares and bursts of radio waves. Consequently, this overview will examine the underlying physics, specifically focusing on the shared principles and unique aspects distinguishing these phenomena for planets and stars respectively.

We examine a Lorentz invariant action formulated as a quadratic function of two rank-2 symmetric tensor fields within Minkowski spacetime. Utilizing 3D rotational symmetry, we perform a scalar-vector-tensor decomposition on these fields and employ a Hamiltonian analysis to categorize models based on possessing exactly seven degrees of freedom. Our study reveals two distinct theories that do not map to linear bigravity in the Hassan-Rosen formalism. In both of these cases, novel mass interaction terms become permissible through transverse diffeomorphism symmetry within the action.

Complex sociological and environmental interactions fuel biological invasions, creating widespread damage across vast geographic areas. For extensive invasive events, traditional optimization methods for directing management efforts often prove ineffective when hampered by computational or data limitations. To address this limitation, this study evaluates an alternative framework that accepts complexity by modeling the invasion as a connected network and employing network architecture to determine optimal management sites via boating decontamination. Situating stations based on 1.6-million boat movements and connecting movements and vessels within Minnesota, the study assesses network-guided strategies against optimized benchmarks across 5,121 lakes and six metropolitan counties by performing a comparative analysis. Researchers found that if information on invading species and boat movements were known in their totality for all areas, the performance of this most useful proposed network-guided index would achieve very high median numbers comparable to optimal 95% to 97% performance. Additionally, the study demonstrates that performance remains comparately effective under different conditions, such as when using distinct network parameters with partial data (averages above 80%, while lower thresholds remain generally acceptable), yet showing greater volatility in these less complete scenarios. Moreover, the overall findings suggest this proposed model is both consistent and capable for large-scale biological management efforts.

We define a Coxeter group as \emph{$\mathbf{a}(2)$-finite} when it possesses a finite number of elements valued by Lusztig's $\mathbf{a}$-function at 2. In this study, for an irreducible group of such type, we provide concrete combinatorial descriptions for the right, two-sided, and left Kazhdan--Lustzyg cells where cells have an $\mathbf{a}$-value of 2. Specifically, by introducing elements termed \emph{studs}, we parameterize the one-sided cells and define these cells using both star operations within weak Bruhat orders. Additionally, this manuscript calculates the total counts of one-sided and two-sided cells.

This work presents a novel and elementary proof of a classical Cheeger theorem, establishing that for any $p \in (1, \infty)$, the existence of a $p$-Poincaré inequality in a metric-measure space implies its $N^{1,p}$ Sobolev space enjoys both the reflexive and separable properties. We further demonstrate separability specifically for the case where $p=1$. Our approach relies on devising a simple construction of an equivalent, uniformly convex norm on the space that relies only on the range $p \in [1, \infty)$. Additionally, when $p \in (1, \infty)$, we provide an explicit functional that is shown to be pointwise equivalent to the least $p$-weak upper gradient.

The virtual detector is a prevalent simulation method for analyzing wavefunction characteristics. Specifically, one variety calculates temporal probability density and currents at specific locations, enabling immediate momentum boundary measurements to bridge quantum and classical domains; however, its incoherent framework presents significant limitations in spectroscopy applications. Conversely, an alternative virtual detector samples the wavefunction's complex value at discrete real-space positions over time, utilizing a Fourier transform to derive energy spectra that are exact under unidirectional propagation but compromised by forward-backward interference otherwise. In this work, we introduce a virtual detector that retains the advantages of coherent measurement while effectively resolving propagation direction and eliminating non-physical interference through a dual-point measurement scheme. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bidirectional approach replicates the exact spectrum within a constant global potential in the continuum limit by reproducing an equivalent wavefunction, confirming the validity and exactness of its spectral output.

The genesis of early supermassive black holes ($\gtrsim 10^9\,M_\odot$ at redshift $z \sim 7$) remains a mystery. While the gravitational collapse of large primordial gas halts shows promise, theory often struggles to model sufficient rapid black hole growth by this means. Focusing on magnetic influences during star formation within atomic-cooling cloud, we employed three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations across various initial magnetic strengths. Results indicate that a primordial magnetic seed is rapidly amplified following the birth of the primary protostar. These strong fields effectively remove angular momentum from the infalling material while boosting accretion rates and elevating fragmentation within unstable gravitationally bound zones. Simultaneously, angular momentum redistribution enhances the merging rate of these fragments. Consequently, nearly all fragments coalesce around the primary object, dramatically increasing the growth rate of the forming star. In this study, we determine magnetic influences to support the direct formation of supermassive stars via the atomic-cooling cloud mechanism.

Boosting predictive accuracy for molecular properties in ab initio simulations is vital for cutting-edge material discovery. However, despite recent advancements integrating machine learning, the application of deep neural networks to enhance quantum chemistry modeling is heavily constrained by the lack of scarce, diverse experimental data points. We demonstrate that training a neural network to replace the exchange-correlation functional within a completely differentiable three-dimensional Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) setup substantially improves simulation reliability. Remarkably, relying on just eight experiment derived data points for diatomic molecules, our exchange-correlation networks achieve superior prediction of atomization energies across 104 molecules, including those with entirely novel atoms and bonding structures absent from the training set.

Tunable intrinsic charge trap capacitive non-volatile flash memory currently dominates the semiconductor market. A key challenge involves generating such intrinsic traps within a dielectric layer without requiring high-temperature processing. Although low-temperature polymer-based solutions have been explored as alternatives, they suffer from rapid performance degradation over successive operational cycles. Furthermore, standard memory architectures rely on tunneling and blocking layers because the primary dielectric or polymer fails to prevent memory leakage on its own. The central challenge in memory cell design is to optimize both leakage current and intrinsic trap density simultaneously. This work presents a tunable flash memory configuration that eliminates the need for separate tunneling and blocking layers by leveraging solution-derived, spin-coated inorganic dielectric films. These films are processible at temperatures at or below 200$^\circ$C while exhibiting low leakage current (below $10$^{-7}$ A.cm$^{-2}$) and high intrinsic charge trap densities (greater than $10$^{12} cm$^{-2}$). Additionally, memory retention is systematically adjustable up to 96% by modulating the trap density as the processing temperature increases.

This study presents a new penalized synthetic control method for evaluating policies. By penalizing the count of predictors employed to generate counterfactuals, the proposed sparse synthetic control aims to enhance pre-treatment fit and identify the most significant predictors. Within a linear factor model framework, theoretical results demonstrating model selection consistency and mean squared error convergence rates are derived. Furthermore, simulation analysis reveals that this sparse approach yields lower bias and superior post-treatment fit compared to unpenalized models, with the technique ultimately applied via a case study assessing the effects of California's Proposition 99 in an environment involving numerous predictors.

While it has long been assumed that random flux cannot trigger a complete metal-insulator phase transition in systems lacking interactions, we demonstrate that this is indeed possible within a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Specifically, we reveal that random flux can induce a transition from a metal band state to an extrinsic higher-order topological insulator—a distinct class characterized by zero-energy modes localized at corners, as opposed to the typical behavior of an Anderson insulator. Using a combination of level statistics and finite-size scaling techniques, we identify these transitions in both metallic and band-insulating states and numerically determine the corresponding critical exponent to be \(\nu = 2.48 \pm 0.08\). Furthermore, we propose a valid band-structure model to elucidate the physical mechanisms of this phase change by utilizing an effective Green's function that is averaged over random fluxes.

Within machine learning, emergent language stands out due to its open-ended nature rather than offering clear-cut problems with defined solutions. Consequently, existing research has primarily been exploratory: focusing on defining new challenges, developing methods, and observing phenomena. However, once these issues are established, future advances depend on studies that can rigorously demonstrate improvements over previous approaches—a type of work we define as systematic research. In this paper, we exemplify this approach in the context of emergent language by first categorizing overarching research goals into engineering and science, and then outlining core methodological aspects of both, analyzing their influence on current work in this field. We conclude with recommendations on applying these principles for progress in emergent language study.

Inertial sensor calibration is becoming increasingly critical for numerous research fields, particularly navigation engineering. Achieving accurate calibration can substantially enhance general navigation capabilities by effectively filtering out both deterministic and stochastic measurement errors inherent to such devices. Although various methods exist for modeling and removing deterministic errors, recent years have seen extensive research focused on modeling stochastic errors due to their complex nature. This typically involves collecting multiple sets (replicates) of error signals, from which a model is identified based on a single representative set. While this approach has improved navigation performance, it currently neglects information contained in the additional replicates recorded by the same sensor. Although distinct external constants during each collection often alter the observed error behavior between repackages, studies suggest that while parameter values differ significantly—likely explaining cause for such shifts— the underlying model structure remains consistent across replicates. This paper examines and investigates properties of methods that combine information from all replicates while accounting for these varying parameter characteristics. Validity is confirmed both through simulations and application to real inertial sensor data by analyzing such phenomena. By integrating knowledge of parameter variations, these approaches not only enhance average navigation precision but also deliver robust estimates regarding uncertainty within the navigation solution.

The dynamic behavior of evolving two-phase flows in bounded regions—assuming equal temperature, incompressibility, and immiscibility—is controlled by the Coupled Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) framework. Furthermore, we prove that these solutions continuously depend on initial and boundary data, thereby confirming weak solution uniqueness. Finally, we confirm the validity of the system for strong solutions as well.
